ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.

Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. 1	## A. Read this first
2	
3	### The answer in six lines
4	
5	1. **What the fund is asking for.** Care that changes the treatment itself between appointments, from a device or biomarker reading, for people who cannot see a specialist often. Part B decodes the wording.
6	2. **What the evidence says.** Outcomes move when a home reading leads to a changed treatment. They mostly do not when the reading is only shown or a reminder is sent. Self-monitoring of blood pressure alone moved pressure by 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling) it moved 6.1 mmHg [D1-01-F05]. An independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication [D1-01-F39]. Part D has the trials, including the ones that failed.
7	3. **Where India's gap is.** The government's hypertension programme controls pressure well in patients who come back, and about half do not come back [D1-03-F10]. In its first nine districts 21.2% of people with high blood pressure are controlled [D1-01-F11]. Parts C, C2 and D2.
8	4. **What to build tonight.** A home blood-pressure step loop: a checked home reading, the state's published step protocol run from a data file, a question on whether the medicine was taken, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Part J is the build pack.
9	5. **Who else does it.** No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings (a search result, not proof of absence). The nearest products abroad are a Japanese cuff maker's UK software that drafts a medication plan for the clinician (search summary only) [D3-06-F35] and US programmes that use their own clinicians [D1-05-F1]. A UK company that dosed one blood-pressure medicine by app was wound up in April 2026 [D3-06-F07]. Parts F1 and H.
10	6. **Who you are pitching to.** The mentor's fund led a 2023 round in Wellthy, an Indian digital-therapeutics company, and its first investment in 2015 was the Japanese company whose blood-pressure app is covered by insurance there [D3-06-F01, D3-06-F26]. That app coaches lifestyle and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. Your loop is the step neither had. Part K.
11	
12	### What you can say at noon, and what you cannot
13	
14	| You can say | You cannot say |
15	|---|---|
16	| Every branch of two published protocols passes our tests. | The product is safe, validated or approved. |
17	| A simulation of ours, built on the programme's own figures, shows where the gain would come from. | The loop improves control. No patient has used it. |

9	### What the evidence says
10	
11	1. **Programmes that change the medicine from home readings work.**
12	   - UK trial TASMIN-SR (552 patients): patients adjusting their own dose by a set plan lowered systolic pressure 9.2 mmHg more than usual care at 12 months (D1-01-F02).
13	   - US trial HyperLink (450 patients): pharmacists adjusting drugs from home readings got 57.2% controlled against 30.0% (D1-01-F04).
14	   - Rural China (33,995 people, 326 villages): village health workers starting and stepping doses by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80 against 19.9% at 18 months. After 4 years, cardiovascular events were lower (hazard ratio 0.75 at age 60 and over, 0.64 under 60), with no difference in falls, low pressure or kidney outcomes (D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38). The programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid village doctors for results, so the protocol is not the only cause.
15	2. **Monitoring and reminders alone do not.**
16	   - Self-monitoring alone, pooled across trials: 1.0 mmHg, no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling): 6.1 mmHg (D1-01-F05).
17	   - A reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 patients): 0.5 mmHg, not significant (D1-01-F06).
18	   - Tuberculosis pillbox trackers (ASCENT, 23,483 patients): no improvement in outcomes (D1-02-F59).
19	   - An independent US review (Peterson Health Technology Institute, October 2024) found that only programmes which adjust medication give clinically meaningful falls in pressure (D1-01-F39).
20	3. **The pattern repeats in other diseases.**
21	   - Warfarin: patients who test at home and change their own dose had fewer clots (risk ratio 0.47) and fewer deaths (0.55). Those who tested at home and phoned the clinic had no fewer deaths (0.94). Each group was compared with usual care, not with the other (D1-02-F05).
22	   - Insulin in type 2 diabetes: a device that computes the next dose cut HbA1c by 1.0 point against 0.3 (D1-01-F13).
23	   - Heart failure: stepping drugs up fast after discharge, with four clinic visits in two months, cut death or readmission at 180 days to an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3%, with more side effects reported (41% against 29%) (D1-01-F27). Two large trials of telemonitoring that left treatment to the usual clinicians or to nurse protocols found no benefit (D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33).
24	4. **India's gap is the dose change and the return visit.**
25	   - Government hypertension programme, 21,895 patients: 51% came back for follow-up. Among those who did, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group (D1-03-F10).
26	   - Tamil Nadu household survey, 6,856 adults: over 95% of diagnosed patients are on treatment, yet control rates were 9.8% for diabetes and 35.4% for hypertension (D1-03-F09). The claims check notes that the paper's summary does not state the denominator for the two control figures.
27	   - Rural community health centres had 79.9% of required posts in four specialities unfilled, as of March 2023 (D1-03-F16). A primary-care consultation lasted about 2 minutes in studies from 2013-2015 (D1-03-F24).
28	5. **Nobody in India was found running a dose-change loop from home readings.** The diabetes programmes sell a sensor plus doctor and coach (D1-04-F02, D1-04-F03, D1-04-F04, D1-04-F05, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07). The protocol model in the government's open-source app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it (D1-06-F40). Phable, the best-known home blood-pressure app, shut in February 2023 (D1-04-F23).
29	6. **Why earlier companies died.** Pear Therapeutics sold its assets for about US$6 million against US$130 million of liabilities (D1-02-F42). Akili earned US$523,000 from prescription sales in 2023 (D1-02-F44). Teva withdrew its sensor inhaler in June 2024 (D1-02-F41). They sold apps or sensors without a payer, and users leave fast: across 93 mental-health apps, the median share still using the app at day 30 was 3.3% (D1-02-F26).

So the value must come from changing the dose between visits and reaching the half who never return. A prompt at a visit that was happening anyway adds nothing.

55	### The three to weigh
56	
57	**1. Home blood-pressure step loop (recommended).**
58	- *What it is.* A home cuff reading goes into an engine that runs India's own published step protocol: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, with a re-check every 30 days, lab values checked before telmisartan is raised, and referral rules for very high readings, abnormal lab values and pregnancy, including women of childbearing age not on effective contraception; the sheet covers adults over 30 (Gujarat protocol, D1-06-F14). The engine proposes the next step. A doctor approves in one tap. The patient gets the change in their own language.
59	- *Why.* The strongest proof of any option, including deaths and strokes avoided at scale by non-physicians. The largest patient pool: 35.5% of Indian adults aged 20 and over have high blood pressure (D1-03-F01). The exact Indian protocol text is public. No Indian service was found.
60	- *Noon demo.* A live reading, the proposal, the approval, the patient message.
61	- *Honest test results.* Every branch of two published protocols passes. A simulated cohort built on the programme's own control-by-step figures from 159,292 patients (D1-06-F04), labelled as a simulation. Reading-quality tests on teammates.
62	- *Main risk.* It can look like "just rules", and the mWellcare result will be raised. The answer: the rules are what the trials show works; nobody runs them at home; the hard parts are trusting a home reading, checking the pills were taken before raising a dose, and proving safety. Who pays is the open business question.
63	
64	**2. Insulin dose guidance for type 2 diabetes.** Strong trials and pharma interest. But no open type 2 simulator exists (D1-06-F30), so tonight's test would be thin, and low blood sugar is a real hazard. Sanofi already has a dosing app (D1-04-F09). Best shown as the second protocol on the same engine, tested on paper.
65	
66	**3. Adaptive home rehabilitation.** The easiest demo. But software rehabilitation only matches in-person care and does not beat usual care (D1-02-F07, D1-02-F54), and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C device licence for cardiac rehabilitation (D1-04-F15).
67	
68	*Also weighed.* Heart failure has strong outcome proof and fits "far from a specialist" best, but it needs lab values, so it cannot be tested honestly tonight; it is the later protocol for the same engine. The breathing plan has the most hardware and the best open data, but the dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor and sensor inhalers failed commercially. Warfarin has the best proof and a small market. Weight-loss injection support is a hot market with no outcome evidence yet and three Indian players already in.

70	### Recommendation
71	
72	Build option 1. Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion.

3	### The recommendation
4	
5	Build the home blood-pressure step loop tonight, and present it as the first protocol on a loop that can carry others. OUR VIEW, for three reasons.
6	
7	1. **It is where the proof is strongest.** When a home reading leads to a medicine change, pressure falls by 5 to 10 mmHg more than usual care in the UK and US trials [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F04]. When health workers were allowed to step doses by protocol in rural China, heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths fell over 4 years with no rise in falls or kidney harm, though that programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38]. An independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication [D1-01-F39].
8	2. **It is where India's gap is.** The government programme gets good control among patients who return, and about half do not return [D1-03-F10]. In its first nine districts 21.2% of people with high blood pressure are controlled [D1-01-F11]. No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the protocol model of the government's open-source app [D1-06-F40].
9	3. **It can be built and tested honestly by noon.** The state protocol is public, down to the doses and the 30-day interval [D1-06-F14]. The programme's own control-by-step figures give a base for a simulated cohort [D1-06-F04]. The build plans are in part J.

11	### The pitch in one breath
12	
13	OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."

17	- **No benefit to patients has been shown.** Tonight's results are code tests, a simulation of our own, and readings from teammates.
18	- **It is not a medical device and not cleared by anyone.** India's July 2026 guidance treats software of this kind as a regulated device, with the class depending on how the condition is graded, and gives no exemption for tools that only a clinician sees [D2-04-F01, D2-04-F03, D2-04-F04, D2-04-F07]. 254	>
255	> *Problem.* India has a simple, published hypertension ladder: amlodipine, then telmisartan, then a diuretic, one step every 30 days. It works for patients who return: in the IHCI cohort, control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% among returners. But only 51% returned, and district control is 21.2%. 256	>

Home readings that drive a medicine change work: pharmacist titration 57% against 30% controlled, and village-doctor protocol titration in China cut cardiovascular events by a quarter. 258	>
259	> *What we built.* A loop that takes a quality-checked home cuff reading (photo or Bluetooth) and runs the state's published protocol, stored as data. The same engine runs the Gujarat and Nigeria protocols with no code change, and an insulin rule on paper.

290	
291	Six questions the notes expect from a deep-tech fund, with short answers.
292	
293	**Software (D2-01)**
294	
295	1. *"This is a rules engine. Where is the deep tech, and what stops Simple copying it?"* The dose logic should be rules, because the evidence comes from protocol titration [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38]. The hard parts are trusting a home reading from any cuff, choosing between stepping up and fixing intake, and a dataset of approved steps with their 30-day response that nobody in India holds [D1-06-F42]. Simple's protocol model stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it [D1-06-F40]; we aim to plug into it.
296	2. *"What measurable impact, and how soon?"* Tonight: code correctness and a simulation only. The endpoint is the share of enrolled patients controlled plus the return rate, against IHCI's 51% return and 21.2% district control [D1-03-F10, D1-01-F11]. A US programme reported -8.7 mmHg at 6 months against education alone, non-randomised, with about 45% dropped out or unreachable [D2-01-F5], so engagement is the number to watch.
297	3. *"Who pays, and is this a medical device?"* Probably a device. CDSCO's software guidance was issued 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01] (D2-01 still had the 21 Oct 2025 draft [D2-01-F11]) and names a hypertension digital therapeutic as device software [D2-04-F07]; the D2-04 note reads a doctor-approved step proposal as Class B, or A, with CDSCO confirming the class [D2-04-F06]. First payer: a private clinic chain at about ₹149 per patient a month (ASSUMPTION), since public drugs cost about ₹200 per patient per year [D2-01-F12].
298	
299	**Hardware (D2-02)**
300	
301	4. *"Your clip measures angles, not heart level."* It compares each reading with a supervised reference posture and catches the two errors with published sizes [D2-02-F16]. Its tolerance is about 1 mmHg of height shift (OUR ARITHMETIC at 0.49 mmHg per cm [D2-02-F17]). Legs, clothing, cuff size and talking are checklist items. Tonight shows only whether it separates deliberately wrong posture on a few teammates.
302	5. *"Patients can photograph an old reading, and the model can misread."* Trained readers reach about 1 mmHg error on good images, but field images are often poor [D2-02-F4] and general models are untested [D2-02-F8]. So reads are shown back, two must agree, memory screens are rejected, a step needs at least 3 days, and the doctor approves. A photo cannot prove who or when; the clip time-join narrows that gap without closing it.
303	6. *"Is a ₹2,000 cuff accurate enough, in Indian arms?"* Use listed cuffs: the HEM-7120 passed ESH-IP 2010 [D2-02-F28]; a popular Indian model is listed as not validated [D2-02-F32]. Cuff size matters more: a regular cuff reads +4.8 mmHg on large arms and +19.5 on extra-large arms [D2-02-F19], so the app asks arm size and refuses out-of-range arms. Validation in Indian populations was not found.
304	
305	### 8. Rung 2: a 2-week test with a doctor in the loop
306	
307	OUR DESIGN, built only from what the notes support. It asks whether the loop survives normal clinic work, not whether it lowers pressure.
308	
309	- **Setting:** one clinic; a small number of adults already on step 1 or 2; their own doctor reviews every proposal in a normal consultation; written consent naming the software, as ICMR's AI guidance expects consent and a human in control [D2-04-F35]. Under the telemedicine guidelines only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and the final prescription or counselling "has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner; clause 5.4) [D2-04-F17]. OUR DESIGN, a question for a lawyer: the approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name.
310	- **Measured:** days with valid readings per patient; proposals raised and how the doctor ruled, with reasons; time to rule; answers to the medicine question; any symptoms reported.
311	- **Must not be used to claim:** any change in pressure or control, safety, or clinical effect. Two weeks is shorter than one 30-day step [D1-06-F14], so few step-ups are expected.
312	- **Ethics:** a desk test on team members is not a clinical investigation on patients [D2-04-F50]. Whether this test counts as research needing an ethics committee is a question to put to the clinic and the university, not something this document decides.
313	
314	So what for us (OUR VIEW): rung 2 answers the first kill question in the spine: do doctors rule on proposals in time.
315	
316	### 9. Rung 3: a 90-day pilot
317	
318	OUR DESIGN throughout unless cited.
319	
320	**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days; patients who stop sending readings count as not controlled. Why: it can move within three 30-day steps; control is what India's programme already reports [D1-01-F11]; and counting silent patients tests the loop where mWellcare did not look, between visits and among the 49% who do not return [D1-01-F46, D1-03-F10].
321	
322	**Secondary measures:** return or engagement rate (valid blocks a month); steps taken; time to approve; adverse events, including dizziness, falls and low readings.
323	
324	**Comparison options:**
325	
326	| Design | Can show | Cannot show |
327	|---|---|---|
328	| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |
329	| Matched clinics | A difference against similar clinics at the same time | Freedom from hidden differences between clinics |
330	| Staggered start (clinics switch on in random order, as in SMARThealth India [D2-01-F16]) | A fairer comparison, each clinic its own control | Quick results: it needs more clinics and time |
331	
332	**Sample size (OUR ARITHMETIC).** Comparing two proportions, 40% controlled against 55% (ASSUMPTION), two-sided 5% significance (z = 1.96), 80% power (z = 0.8416):
333	
334	- p-bar = (0.40 + 0.55) / 2 = 0.475; 2 x 0.475 x 0.525 = 0.49875; square root = 0.7062
335	- 0.40 x 0.60 + 0.55 x 0.45 = 0.24 + 0.2475 = 0.4875; square root = 0.6982
336	- n per arm = (1.96 x 0.7062 + 0.8416 x 0.6982)^2 / (0.15)^2 = (1.3842 + 0.5876)^2 / 0.0225 = 3.8880 / 0.0225 = 172.8, so 173
337	- With 20% drop-out (ASSUMPTION): 173 / 0.8 = 216.3, so **217 per arm, 434 in all**
338	
339	This assumes patients are randomised one by one. Randomising by clinic would need more patients; that is not computed here. D2-01's earlier sketch was about 300 patients over 6 months (OUR DESIGN).
340	
341	**Approvals and registrations (from D2-04):** a Form MD-13 test licence covers software made "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]; a clinical investigation of an investigational device on patients needs CLA permission on Form MD-22/MD-23 [D2-04-F14, D2-04-F39]; an ethics committee approval and CTRI registration before the first patient [D2-04-F45]. Whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides each change counts as a clinical investigation is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Data duties under the DPDP Rules start on 13 May 2027 by the gazette's wording (one law firm says a day earlier), inside a pilot that starts now [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20]. No Indian legal basis was found for a nurse or community health officer changing doses [D2-04-F18].
342	
343	**Budget lines** (OUR ARITHMETIC, 217 loop-arm patients, 3 months, prices from the notes):
344	
345	| Line | Unit | Total |
346	|---|---|---|
347	| Cuffs (HEM-7120) | ₹1,849-2,334 each [D2-02-F30] | ₹4,01,233-5,06,478 |
348	| Messages (WhatsApp) | ₹15 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION in D2-01; price not searched) | ₹9,765 |
349	| Health worker calls to silent patients | ₹30 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION; D2-01: ₹25,000 / 9,600 minutes x 5 = about ₹13, rounded up) | ₹19,530 |
350	| Cloud and photo reading | ₹7 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION) | ₹4,557 |
351	| **Total** | | **about ₹4.35-5.40 lakh (OUR ARITHMETIC)** |
352	
353	Not included: doctor time, licence and ethics fees (not found in the notes), team costs.
354	
355	**Three results that would make the team stop (OUR VIEW):**
356	1. Doctors leave most proposals unruled for days, so the loop stalls.
357	2. Most enrolled patients stop sending valid blocks within the first month (the US programme lost about 45% over its course [D2-01-F5]).
358	3. Any serious harm linked to an approved step, such as symptomatic low pressure or a fall, that the safety branches did not catch.
359	
360	### 10. So what for us
361	
362	OUR VIEW:
363	- Tonight's win is a tested loop that a human approves, plus a simulation that honestly says the gain comes from contact. Do not trade that for a bigger claim.
364	- The 135/85 home mapping is our design; say it before a mentor does.
365	- Rung 2 is the real next step: one clinic, two weeks, with the ethics question put to the clinic and university on day one.
366	- The 90-day pilot needs about 434 patients if randomised one by one (OUR ARITHMETIC), more by clinic, and an answer from counsel. Budget time for that before money.

183	### The frameworks, applied to the home blood-pressure step loop
184	
185	This section applies the venture course's frameworks to card 1. Facts carry IDs; every target, price and rating is ours and is labelled.
186	
187	#### S.M.A.R.T problem statement
188	
189	To stop blood pressure staying high because the dose change waits for a visit that half the patients never make [R], doctors in private clinics and their patients on blood-pressure medicine [S] need the 30-day review done from home, as a doctor-approved next step of the published protocol [A], shown in one clinic over a 90-day pilot [T], measured by the share of patients under 140/90 and bought at ₹149 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION) [M].
190	
191	- **S · Specific:** one buyer (a hypothesis) and one gap: the dose step between visits.
192	- **M · Measurable:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned. The price is an ASSUMPTION.
193	- **A · Action-oriented:** each cycle ends in one action: step up, support, order tests, refer or hold.
194	- **R · Relevant:** 51% returned; control among them rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
195	- **T · Time-bound:** a prototype by noon on 14 November 2026; a pilot endpoint at 90 days.
196	
197	#### The belief we turn upside down
198	
199	- **Belief we turn over:** a medicine dose can change only when the patient is in front of the doctor.
200	- **Instead:** the reading travels to the doctor and the decision travels home. The 30-day review happens whether or not the patient returns.
201	
202	Why we think this solves the problem (OUR VIEW):
203	
204	- The step that fails in India is the return visit, not the protocol [D1-03-F10].

3	### What this part shows
4	
5	This part names, for each stage of a therapy loop, the technology that exists in November 2026, its cost and testing, and what a student team can build by noon. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.

7	### The parts of a therapy loop
8	
9	A loop that changes treatment has six stages.

11	| Stage | Its job | Technology found | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
12	|---|---|---|---|
13	| Sense | Get a number from the patient's home | Omron cuffs read with omblepy [D1-06-F07]; cuff-screen photo readers [D2-02-F4]; Bluetooth glucose profile [D1-06-F29] | Photo of any cuff, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
14	| Check the reading | Was it taken properly? | AHA and ESH home rules [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11]; posture-error trials [D2-02-F16] | Kit-built motion clip plus a checklist |
15	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed next step | Step protocols [D1-06-F14]; HL7 CQL [D2-03-F52]; OpenAPS bounds [D2-03-F46] | One YAML file per protocol, run by a pure `decide()` function |
16	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | CDS Hooks cards with an accept button [D2-03-F53] | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
17	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram bot [D2-01-F9]; Indian speech APIs [D2-03-F58] | Telegram chat plus a web form |
18	| Learn | Improve choices from each patient's response | Personal drug-response trials [D2-03-F12]; adaptive message timing [D2-03-F10] | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |

49	### Making a home reading trustworthy
50	
51	A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff. This section gives the guidance, the size of each mistake, the home threshold, and the clip that catches what a sensor can see.
52	
53	**The guidance.** AHA: at least 5 minutes of quiet seated rest, two readings at least 1 minute apart, morning before tablets and evening, 7 days or more (minimum 3) [D2-02-F10]. ESH: the same, "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Dropping day 1 is "a matter of debate" for the ESH [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10]. The ESH warns monitors over 4 years old drift [D2-02-F13] and calls handwritten logs "often incomplete and inaccurate" [D2-02-F14].
54	
55	**The size of each mistake** (systolic / diastolic, mmHg):
56	
57	| Mistake | Effect | Source |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| Arm on lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover, n = 133, Baltimore) | [D2-02-F16] |
60	| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) | [D2-02-F16] |
61	| Arm below heart level | +0.49 / +0.47 per cm; arm at desk height against heart height +6.1 / +5.7 (n = 128) | [D2-02-F17] |
62	| Back not supported | +5 to +15 / +6 (AHA); +6 to +10 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F18, D2-02-F20] |
63	| Legs crossed | +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 | [D2-02-F18] |
64	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large one | +4.8 systolic (randomised crossover, n = 195) | [D2-02-F19] |
65	| Regular cuff on an arm that needs an extra-large one | +19.5 systolic | [D2-02-F19] |
66	| Talking | +10 / +10 (older table, no citations in it) | [D2-02-F20] |
67	| Cuff over clothing | +5 to +50 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F20] |
68	| No rest instead of 5 minutes | No meaningful difference below 140 systolic; none to at least 4 mmHg above (secondary review) | [D2-02-F21] |

70	The HEM-7120 standard cuff fits arms of 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30], so arm size must be measured.
71	
72	**Home against clinic thresholds.** The ESH says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the ISH [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines on Hypertension IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use 135/85 at home. The Gujarat protocol is written for clinic readings at 140/90 [D1-06-F14]. Our engine (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-01-F1]) measures on days 24-30 of each 30-day cycle, counts a session only if both readings pass the quality check, needs 3 valid days, drops day 1 only when 4 or more remain, calls the block "still high" at a mean of 135 or 85, and sends any confirmed session at 180 or 110 to urgent review. Using a clinic protocol on home readings is our choice and must be said on the slide.
73	
74	Why it matters: SMARThealth India (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].
75	
76	**The kit-built quality clip** (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F16, D2-02-F17]). An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff and the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once and the clip stores that posture. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest (restarting on movement), checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture, requires stillness through a 60-second measurement, and enforces 60 seconds between readings. A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2). It shows green or red and posts reasons, joined to the reading by time. Legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, bladder and smoking go into a 4-question phone checklist. Thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE.
77	
78	![The reading-quality clip on the upper arm and forearm, with its green and red states](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)
79	*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*
80	
81	So what for us (OUR VIEW): the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.

83	### Algorithms that set a dose
84	
85	Four families of dose algorithm are in use; each is bounded.
86	
87	**Closed-loop insulin, the model case.** Control-IQ (randomised 2:1, 168 people with type 1 diabetes, USA, 6 months, against a sensor-augmented pump) raised time in the target glucose range by 11 points and cut HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) by 0.33, with one ketoacidosis case [D1-01-F24]. In insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 2IQP (randomised 2:1, 319 adults, US and Canada, 13 weeks, both arms on a glucose sensor, maker-funded) cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points [D1-01-F43]. The do-it-yourself system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down [D2-03-F46]:
88	- It acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the core version "cannot issue insulin boluses".
89	- The temporary rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate".
90	- Missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan.
91	
92	Its code (oref0, MIT) says it is "not a 'set and forget' system" [D1-06-F12]; dosing logic sits in `determine-basal.js` [D1-06-F53].
93	
94	**Insulin titration rules.** ADA 2025: start basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, "increase 2 units every 3 days to reach FPG target without hypoglycemia", and if low sugar has no clear reason "lower dose by 10-20%" [D1-06-F16]. An upper limit of 0.5 units/kg/day is quoted (search summary only) [D1-06-F18]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. d-Nav (randomised, 181 adults with type 2 diabetes, 3 US centres, 6 months, device plus clinician against clinician alone) cut HbA1c 1.0% against 0.3% with equal low-sugar events; several authors were maker staff or shareholders [D1-01-F13]. TeleDiab-2 (randomised, 191 adults starting basal insulin, France, 4 months) cut HbA1c 1.44% and 1.48% against 0.92% [D1-01-F14]. The FDA has cleared dose apps such as My Dose Coach (2017) and iSage Rx (2024) [D2-03-F47]. A reinforcement-learning model, RL-DITR, was tested only single-arm in 16 inpatients in China [D2-03-F11].
95	
96	**Blood-pressure protocols.** Gujarat's ladder, with 30-day reviews: amlodipine 5 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, add telmisartan 40 mg, telmisartan 80 mg (after blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein; if any is abnormal, refer, or, with no specialist reachable, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone), add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, then check adherence and refer; the sheet covers adults over 30, checks adherence at each visit, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception [D1-06-F14]. Punjab and Maharashtra differ at step 2 [D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]; across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82% [D1-06-F04]. People do differ: PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden, 1,468 treatment periods) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].
97	
98	**Warfarin tables.** The IWPC algorithm sets only the starting dose [D2-03-F48]. Feedback tables agree on no change at INR (a clotting test) 2.0-3.0 but differ outside it (search summary only) [D1-06-F37]. Self-management cut clots (RR 0.47) and deaths (RR 0.55) in pooled trials, compared indirectly with self-testing [D1-02-F05].
99	
100	| Algorithm | Input | Output | How it is bounded |
101	|---|---|---|---|
102	| Closed-loop insulin | Continuous glucose sensor | Temporary basal rate | Rate caps, no boluses (oref0), revert on missing data [D2-03-F46] |
103	| Basal titration | Fasting glucose over 3 days | +2 units or -10-20% | Upper limit per kg; hypo branch; clinician sets cause [D1-06-F16, D1-06-F18] |
104	| BP ladder | 30-day review of readings | Next written regimen | Fixed steps, lab and pregnancy guards, referral at the end [D1-06-F14] |
105	| Warfarin table | INR | Weekly dose change in % | No-change band 2.0-3.0; hold at high INR [D1-06-F37] |
106	
107	So what for us (OUR VIEW): every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing. A ladder is the simplest case. PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.
108	
109	### A protocol as data
110	
111	A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch, and swapped without changing the engine. This section gives the prior art, what Indian decision-support trials found, and how our files fit.
112	
113	**Prior art.** A 2002 review of 11 guideline languages found four basic parts: data collection, decision, patient state, intervention [D2-03-F54]. WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit; the blood-pressure kit is for pregnancy only, its machine-readable layers are "not yet available", and its licence is non-commercial [D2-03-F50, D2-03-F51]. HL7 CQL is a standard logic language with an Apache-2.0 engine that is "not a complete implementation" and needs a Java 17 translator [D2-03-F52]. CDS Hooks returns suggestion cards with an accept button (CC BY 4.0) [D2-03-F53]. India's open Simple app (MIT, alive 4 Nov 2026) stores a protocol as a drug list plus `follow_up_days`; no step logic was found in its protocol model [D1-06-F40].
114	
115	**Indian decision-support trials.**
116	
117	| Trial | Design and setting | Compared | Result |
118	|---|---|---|---|
119	| CARRS [D2-03-F14] | Randomised, 1,146 with diabetes, urban clinics, India and Pakistan, 28 months | Coordinators plus decision-support records against usual care | Positive: composite goal 18.2% against 8.1% |
120	| mWellcare [D2-03-F15] | Cluster randomised, 40 health centres, 3,698 people, 12 months | Nurse-run app with decision support against enhanced usual care | Null: systolic -0.98 (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67) |
121	| mPower Heart [D2-03-F16] | Before-and-after, no control, Himachal Pradesh, 6,797 people | Phone tool drafts prescription, physician vets | Systolic -14.6 mmHg, uncontrolled |
122	| SMARThealth India [D2-03-F17] | Stepped-wedge cluster, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh | Health-worker tablet plus doctor decision support against usual care | Null on blood pressure |
123	| IMPACT Diabetes [D2-03-F18] | Cluster randomised, 8 centres, 418 people, 9 months | Health-worker decision support under physician supervision | Small positive: HbA1c fall of 0.5% or more, 21.8% against 10.3% |
124	
125	**The test-coverage lesson.** When the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].
126	
127	**How our files fit** (OUR DESIGN, detail in part J). One YAML file per protocol (Gujarat, Nigeria, and the ADA insulin rule as paper only), each number carrying the exact source words; a missing value is `null` and the engine refuses that branch [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15, D1-06-F16]. A pure `decide()` function checks safety first, then enough readings, the 30-day interval, the threshold, adherence, the last step, and the lab and pregnancy guards, and only then proposes a step. It never computes a dose; it only picks a regimen written in the file. Thirty-six test cases cover every branch listed so far, run against two protocols; the age, childbearing-age, abnormal-lab and "outside the demo" branches found later on the sheets still need tests (part J) [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15].
128	
129	So what for us (OUR VIEW): decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so our engine must act between visits, not prompt during them. ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.

131	### Adaptive nudging, bandits and reinforcement learning
132	
133	Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. A just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) adapts "weekly, daily, or even many times a day"; a micro-randomised trial randomises each decision point [D2-03-F01].
134	
135	| Study | Design | Result |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| HeartSteps V1 [D2-03-F02] | Micro-randomised, 44 US adults, 6 weeks | Any suggestion +35 steps in 30 minutes (p = .06), fading over time; walking suggestions +59 (p = .02) |
138	| HeartSteps V2 [D2-03-F03]; Oralytics [D2-03-F08] | Learning algorithms deployed in US trials | Outcome results NOT FOUND |
139	| DIAMANTE [D2-03-F10] | Randomised, 3 arms, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months | Learned texts beat random texts: steps up 19% against 1.6% (random) and 3.9% (weekly message); HbA1c not in the abstract |
140	| Automated diabetes prevention app [D2-03-F42] | Randomised non-inferiority, 368 people, 2 US sites, 12 months | Matched human coaches: 31.7% against 31.9% |
141	| JITAI meta-analyses [D2-03-F04, D2-03-F06] | Mental health, 23 studies; sleep, 11 trials | Small effect (g = 0.15); adaptive not better than non-adaptive for sleep |
142	
143	Two cautions. Standard estimators "can be inconsistent and fail to be replicable" on bandit-trial data [D2-03-F09]. A 2026 guideline for live learning systems uses pre-set fallbacks, which "safeguarded participants" in two case studies [D2-03-F07].
144	
145	Open tools: MABWiser (Apache 2.0) [D1-06-F55]; Open Bandit Pipeline (Apache 2.0, off-policy estimators) [D2-03-F49]; HeartSteps V1 data (CC BY 4.0, 8,274 decisions) [D1-06-F44].
146	
147	So what for us (OUR VIEW): adaptive timing has one head-to-head win, on steps, not a clinical measure. In our loop it could help complete 7-day reading blocks, later. A HeartSteps replay shows the method only.

149	### Personal response models and "digital twins"
150	
151	A "digital twin" here is a model of one person that predicts their response to food or treatment.
152	
153	- **Twin Health, India, blood pressure** [D2-03-F19]: secondary analysis of an Indian randomised trial in 319 people with type 2 diabetes (233 twin, 86 standard care). Home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes. Systolic fell 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg at one year. Limits: secondary analysis, only 59 people on blood-pressure drugs, company-linked. The drug changes followed a protocol; the machine learning predicted diet response.
154	- **Method** [D2-03-F21]: predicts each person's post-meal glucose from a glucose sensor, food logs and other inputs and "dynamically adjusts dietary recommendations". No open code found.
155	- **Twin Health, US** [D2-03-F43]: randomised, 150 people, Cleveland Clinic, 12 months; HbA1c under 6.5% without glucose drugs other than metformin in 71% against 2.4%. Source is the institution's summary; funding not shown.
156	- **Twin Health, real world** [D2-03-F20]: 1,853 completers, HbA1c -1.8%, no control (THEIR CLAIM).
157	- **Glucose foundation models**: GluFormer (over 10 million readings, 10,812 adults) predicted later diabetes and cardiovascular death (arXiv only) [D2-03-F23]; CGM-LSM and GlucoFM report lower forecast error [D2-03-F24].
158	- **Blood pressure**: one agent-based model simulates six drugs on virtual patients; licence unconfirmed (search summary only) [D1-06-F43].
159	
160	PHYSIC measured personal response over repeated periods [D2-03-F12]; a single run-in response did not predict the long-term one [D2-03-F13].
161	
162	So what for us (OUR VIEW): no open twin exists for blood-pressure drugs. Each approved step in our loop gives one labelled example (readings before, readings 30 days after). That is the dataset a response model would need, and it does not exist in the open today [D1-06-F42].

197	**The design pattern** (OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]):
198	1. The model handles language only: cuff photo to strict JSON, translation, speech.
199	2. A fixed, tested engine makes every decision, from the protocol file.
200	3. Code checks every output against the protocol: plausible ranges, two agreeing reads, a regimen that exists in the file.
201	4. A clinician approves every change.

270	### So what for us
271	
272	OUR VIEW.
273	- **The reading is the science.** Arm position alone adds 3.9-6.5 mmHg [D2-02-F16], and noisy readings broke an Indian trial [D2-03-F17]. The clip and reading rules are our deep-tech claim, not the rules engine.
274	- **Bound every action.** Copy OpenAPS [D2-03-F46]: choose only written regimens, hold the current step on missing data, never step on one reading.
275	- **Keep models on language.** A constrained model still made dangerous dose errors 1% of the time [D2-03-F38]; it reads photos and speaks Hindi, and the engine decides.
276	- **Act between visits, not during them.** Decision support used during clinic visits did not beat good usual care in India [D2-03-F15, D2-03-F17]; our value is the change made without a visit.
277	- **The learning layer is earned, not claimed.** People do respond differently to drugs [D2-03-F12], but no open data exists to model it; each approved step we log builds it.

12	|---|---|---|
13	| 1. Does the loop work? | Abroad, yes, in randomised trials. US, HyperLink: 450 adults, pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings against usual care, 57.2% against 30.0% controlled at 6 and 12 months [D1-01-F04]. Lesotho: 547 adults, lay workers adjusting one pill with an app against referral to a clinic, 58% against 48% controlled at 12 months [D3-05-F24]. India's nearest trial was null: mWellcare, 3,698 people at 40 health centres, 12 months, a decision-support app at the visit against enhanced usual care, systolic (the upper number) 0.98 mmHg apart, not significant [D1-01-F46]. 14	| 2. Is the gap real in India? | Yes. At 24 government-programme clinics 51% of 21,895 registered patients returned; among them control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% (no comparison group) [D1-03-F10]. 3	### G1. What this part shows
4	
5	This part tests the home blood-pressure step loop as a strategy partner and an early-stage deep-tech investor would: one governing question, the choices, money, forces, risks and the next 90 days. Claims-check corrections (D3-01 to D3-03) are applied; judgements carry OUR VIEW.

7	### G2. The question tree
8	
9	The governing question: "Can a medicine-adjusting loop that starts with blood pressure become a business that improves outcomes for people far from a specialist?" Six sub-questions follow, each graded strong, partial or missing.
10	
11	| Sub-question | What the research supports | Evidence |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| 1. Does the loop work? | Abroad, yes, in randomised trials. US, HyperLink: 450 adults, pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings against usual care, 57.2% against 30.0% controlled at 6 and 12 months [D1-01-F04]. Lesotho: 547 adults, lay workers adjusting one pill with an app against referral to a clinic, 58% against 48% controlled at 12 months [D3-05-F24]. India's nearest trial was null: mWellcare, 3,698 people at 40 health centres, 12 months, a decision-support app at the visit against enhanced usual care, systolic (the upper number) 0.98 mmHg apart, not significant [D1-01-F46]. No Indian randomised trial of the home loop was found (D1-01). | Strong abroad; missing in India |
14	| 2. Is the gap real in India? | Yes. At 24 government-programme clinics 51% of 21,895 registered patients returned; among them control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% (no comparison group) [D1-03-F10]. The cause is less clear: of 157 lapsed patients phoned in Bathinda (not a random sample), 24.8% felt no illness and 22.2% named distance [D3-05-F07]. | Strong on size; partial on cause |
15	| 3. Can it be delivered safely and legally? | Safety: in rural China (33,995 people, 4 years) dose-stepping by village doctors under physician supervision brought no more falls, low pressure or kidney harm than in comparison villages [D1-01-F38]. Law: CDSCO (India's device regulator) lists hypertension platforms as medical device software (July 2026 guidance) [D2-04-F07]; the risk class and the pilot permit are questions for counsel and CDSCO [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F14]. The 2020 telemedicine guidelines say only a registered doctor may prescribe and must deliver the prescription directly [D2-04-F17]. No order letting a nurse change a dose was found [D2-04-F18]. | Partial |
16	| 4. Will anyone pay? | No Indian payer was found paying for remote monitoring or digital therapy as a line item [D2-04-F47]. Our ₹149 a month is an ASSUMPTION (DT3). | Missing |
17	| 5. Can it be defended? | Not yet. The protocol is public [D1-06-F14]. The government programme (over 2.5 million patients by April 2022) runs on the open-source Simple app, whose protocol model has no step ladder [D2-01-F12, D1-06-F40]. | Missing |
18	| 6. Can this team start it? | The prototype, yes: the protocol and open readings exist [D1-06-F14, D2-03-F61]. A pilot needs a supervising doctor, an ethics committee and prior registration (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]; the team has none yet. | Partial |

103

117	### G10. Three questions a partner would press
118	
119	Each has the honest answer and what would settle it.
120	
121	1. **"Is this a dose product or a follow-up product?"** On clinic data, mostly follow-up: among programme patients who kept attending, later steps added 6-7 points of control to the first pill's 70-76% (OUR ARITHMETIC: 77 - 70; 82 - 76) [D1-06-F04]. Home data may show more: of 1,920 treated attenders in 12 states, 21.8% looked controlled in clinic but not at home [D3-04-F09]. Settled by: a pilot that counts patients brought back separately from doses changed.
122	2. **"Who pays, and does that buyer serve the patient the challenge names?"** Nobody yet [D2-04-F47]. ₹1,788 a year (₹149 a month) adds about 46% to one private-brand pill's ₹3,906 (OUR ARITHMETIC: 1,788 ÷ 3,906) [D2-05-F17]; the rural patient sits in the public tier, assumed at ₹15 a month (DT3). 124	
125	So what for us (OUR VIEW): no answer to question 2 in 90 days means a public-good tool, not a company.

14	| "continuously personalise care" | Recompute the treatment from this patient's readings: protocol step, response to the last step, medicine taken or not, what is unsafe. | Gujarat's hypertension sheet: "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" [D1-06-F14]. |

The specialist owns the protocol and sees the exceptions. | 79.9% of required specialist posts at rural community health centres were unfilled (B8) [D1-03-F16]. |
18	| "beyond monitoring and reminders" | Reach adaptive depth 4: the therapy itself changes. | Self-monitoring alone: 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling): 6.1 (B6) [D1-01-F05]. |

20	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the fund asks for a routine treatment decision between visits, from a home reading, by someone the patient can reach.
