22	### B3. What "beyond monitoring and reminders" rules in and out
23	
24	This document scores every product on an "adaptive depth" scale from 0 to 4. The fund names levels 1 and 2. OUR VIEW: it is asking for level 4.
25	
26	| Level | Examples in the notes | What the evidence shows |
27	|---|---|---|
28	| 0: uses no patient data | Nerivio migraine wearable, switched on by the patient, rated 0-1 [D1-02-F12]. India: none rated 0 | Nothing adapts. |
29	| 1: shows data | India: pocket ECGs (search summary only) [D1-04-F32]. Abroad: Omron VitalSight [D1-01-F39] | Self-monitoring alone: no effect [D1-01-F05]; one exception, a glucose sensor, in part D [D1-01-F42]. |
30	| 2: reminders, generic content | India: government Simple app, with overdue lists and reminder messages [D3-05-F03]. Abroad: Medisafe reminder app | Medisafe, 411 US adults, 12 weeks, against control: 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. |
31	| 3: coaching from the person's own data | India: Sugar.fit, BeatO, Fitterfly [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Abroad: CureApp HT, Japan | CureApp HT, 390 untreated patients, 12 weeks, against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour systolic 2.4 mmHg lower [D1-01-F07]. |
32	| 4: changes the therapy (dose, protocol step, exercise prescription) | India: only Sanofi's My Dose Coach found, its Indian results unconfirmed [D1-04-F09]. Abroad: d-Nav; insulin pumps [D1-05-F41] | d-Nav dose device (maker-linked authors), 181 US insulin users, 6 months, against clinician support alone: HbA1c (three-month average sugar) down 1.0 point against 0.3 [D1-01-F13]. |
33	
34	**The line between 3 and 4.** Level 3 changes the advice: what to eat, how to exercise. Level 4 changes the prescription: a new dose or protocol step. A clinician approving each change keeps it at level 4. Indian diabetes programmes sit at 3: no page says sensor data changes a drug dose [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The test: after the software runs, the prescription is different.
35	
36	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: level 4 is the entry condition, however good the sensor.
37	
38	### B4. The loop: sense, decide, confirm, act, learn
39	
40	Five stages: what happens at each, and where existing products stop.
41	
42	![Monitoring against a therapy loop](adaptive-care-pictures/00-the-loop.png)
43	
44	*Diagram: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop changes the treatment.*
45	
46	- **Sense.** A home device gives a number, valid only if taken correctly. Level 1 products stop here (B3).
47	- **Decide.** Software applies a written protocol to this patient's readings and proposes the next step. Coaching apps decide advice, not doses [D1-04-F04]; the protocol model of the government's Simple app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step ladder was found in it [D1-06-F40].
48	- **Confirm.** A doctor, nurse or health worker approves each change; unsafe cases go to a specialist. Trials used pharmacists [D1-01-F04] or village doctors [D1-01-F09]; no Indian service doing this from home readings was found [D1-04-F09].
49	- **Act.** The patient gets the new dose, medicine or exercise level. Heart-failure telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol found no benefit (B6).
50	- **Learn.** The next readings show whether it worked, and the loop runs again. At 24 government-programme sites, 10,621 of 21,895 patients did not return [D1-03-F10].
51	
52	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: India lacks decide, confirm and act between visits.
53	
54	### B5. A map of feedback-driven therapies
55	
56	Five kinds, by what the loop changes.
57	
58	| What changes | Home signal | How fast it responds | Proof | Who decides |
59	|---|---|---|---|---|
60	| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (clotting test), weight | Days to weeks: insulin every 3 days in a 2025 US rule [D1-06-F16]; blood pressure re-checked at 30 days [D1-06-F14] | Strong: randomised trials with fewer deaths, clots or hospital stays [D1-01-F38, D1-01-F27, D1-02-F05] | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04, D1-02-F06, D1-01-F09] |
61	| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Each meal [D1-01-F22] | Mixed: a company-linked Indian trial cut HbA1c 2.9 points against 0.3 with standard care (319 people, 1 year) [D1-01-F19]; a US review of type 2 tools without a continuous sensor was negative (B7) [D1-01-F40] | App, coach |
62	| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Each session [D1-06-F36] | Matches in-person care; no better than usual care (pooled stroke trials, 661 people) [D1-02-F07] | Therapist or app [D1-02-F54] |
63	| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Automatic | Strong: against a sensor alone, a dose algorithm cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points (319 adults with type 2 diabetes, US and Canada, 13 weeks, Tandem-funded) [D1-01-F43] | Algorithm, within clinician-set limits [D1-05-F41] |
64	| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | During practice [D1-02-F15] | Weak: guided breathing had no blood-pressure effect once maker-linked trials were excluded (8 trials, 494 people) [D1-02-F11] | Patient |
65	
66	OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none. A student team, and a low-resource country, should start there.
67	
68	### B6. Five rules the evidence gives
69	
70	OUR VIEW: five rules, each with the numbers behind it.
71	
72	**1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring alone lowered systolic pressure 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, 6.1 [D1-01-F05]. Two US heart-failure trials of remote monitoring without a mandated dose protocol (1,653 and 1,437 patients, 180 days) found no benefit [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33]. Fast dose stepping after discharge cut readmission or death (B7) [D1-01-F27]. Against usual care, warfarin patients who set their own dose from home tests had fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.55, 8 trials); in 3 separate trials, those who left the dose to the clinic did not (0.94); the two approaches were not compared head to head [D1-02-F05].
73	
74	**2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In a UK trial (1,182 patients, 12 months), sending readings electronically added a non-significant 1.2 mmHg over paper once the family doctor adjusted doses [D1-01-F03]. In rural China (33,995 people, 18 months), supervised village doctors stepping drugs by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80, against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. At 4 years cardiovascular events were lower (hazard ratio 0.75 at age 60 and over), though the programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid incentives [D1-01-F38].
75	
76	**The Indian null result belongs here.** mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension or diabetes, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: no Indian randomised trial tested that (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
77	
78	**3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children gave 84% adherence against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.
79	
80	**4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Apps and sensors sold on their own failed. Pear's assets fetched just over $6 million against $130 million of liabilities (2023-2024) [D1-02-F42]; Teva stopped US distribution of its sensor inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41]. Those at scale are paid by employers and insurers for clinician-led programmes (Hinge Health: revenue $234.970 million in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]) or sell a therapy device (Insulet: $842.0 million [D1-05-F41]).
81	
82	**5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In 8 remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants) median retention was 5.5 days. Clinician referral added 40 days [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.
83	
84	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: B10 turns these rules into a test for any idea.
85	
86	### B7. What "measurable" means
87	
88	One endpoint per condition that a pilot could read at about 90 days.
89	
90	| Condition | Endpoint | Effect the trials found | "Clinically meaningful" threshold |
91	|---|---|---|---|
92	| High blood pressure | Share under 140/90 [D1-06-F03] | 57.2% controlled with pharmacist dose changes from home readings, against 30.0% with usual care (450 US patients, at both 6 and 12 months) [D1-01-F04] | 5 mmHg systolic against usual care [D1-01-F39] |
93	| Type 2 diabetes on insulin | HbA1c | Down 1.44-1.48 points with daily dose proposals, against 0.92 with standard care (191 adults, France, 4 months) [D1-01-F14] | None given; a US review judged 0.23-0.60 points not meaningful for type 2 tools without a continuous sensor [D1-05-F4] |
94	| Diabetes with a sensor | Time in range | Up 14 points with a dose algorithm (B5) [D1-01-F43] | NOT RESEARCHED |
95	| Heart failure | Readmission or death | 15.2% against 23.3% at 180 days with fast dose stepping after discharge (1,078 patients, 14 countries; adjusted estimates; side effects 41% against 29%) [D1-01-F27] | NOT RESEARCHED |
96	| Warfarin | Time in the target INR range | Trials against usual care report clots (risk ratio 0.47) and deaths (0.55) instead [D1-02-F05] | NOT RESEARCHED |
97	
98	No blood-pressure dose-change trial in our first-round notes reported before 6 months [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04].
99	
100	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: for blood pressure, measure the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned.
101	
102	### B8. What "cannot access frequent specialist support" means in India
103	
104	Five numbers show the gap.
105	
106	1. **79.9%**: required posts in four specialities (surgery, medicine, obstetrics, paediatrics) unfilled at rural community health centres, March 2023 [D1-03-F16].
107	2. **About 650** endocrinologists and **4,000** cardiologists, 2017 count (search summary only) [D1-03-F18].
108	3. **About 2 minutes**: a primary-care consultation, 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24].
109	4. **51%**: of 21,895 patients at 24 government hypertension programme sites returned for follow-up, 2018-2019 [D1-03-F10].
110	5. **9.8%**: diabetes control rate in a Tamil Nadu survey (denominator not stated), though over 95% of diagnosed patients were on treatment (6,856 adults, 2025 paper) [D1-03-F09].
111	
112	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the scarce thing is the prescriber's decision, which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make.
113	
114	### B9. Terms used in this document
115	
116	- **Adaptive depth:** 0-4 score for how far a product changes treatment.
117	- **Adherence:** taking the medicine as prescribed.
118	- **Closed loop:** a device that measures and adjusts therapy itself.
119	- **Digital therapeutic:** software that changes one patient's treatment.
120	- **Endpoint:** the result a trial is judged on.
121	- **Hazard ratio:** a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events.
122	- **HbA1c:** blood test of average sugar over about three months.
123	- **INR:** clotting test that sets the warfarin dose.
124	- **Not significant:** small enough to be chance (a null result).
125	- **Protocol:** a written step-by-step treatment plan.
126	- **Randomised trial:** people get treatments by chance.
127	- **Risk ratio:** risk with treatment divided by risk without; below 1 means lower risk.
128	- **Systolic:** the upper blood-pressure number, in mmHg (millimetres of mercury).
129	- **Time in range:** share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL.
130	- **Titration:** stepping a dose towards a target.
131	
132	### B10. So what for us
133	
134	OUR VIEW. Any idea must pass three questions.
135	
136	1. **What changes?** After a home reading the prescription is different (level 4), within days.
137	2. **Who decides?** A general doctor, nurse or health worker, under a written protocol; unsafe cases go to a specialist.
138	3. **What moves, and who pays?** One endpoint passes an accepted threshold in 90 days, and a named payer wants it.

17	| "patients who cannot access frequent specialist support" | Move the routine decision to a general doctor, nurse or health worker under a written protocol. The specialist owns the protocol and sees the exceptions. | 79.9% of required specialist posts at rural community health centres were unfilled (B8) [D1-03-F16]. |
18	| "beyond monitoring and reminders" | Reach adaptive depth 4: the therapy itself changes. | Self-monitoring alone: 1.0 mmHg; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling): 6.1 (B6) [D1-01-F05]. |
19	
20	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the fund asks for a routine treatment decision between visits, from a home reading, by someone the patient can reach.
21	
22	### B3. What "beyond monitoring and reminders" rules in and out
23	
24	This document scores every product on an "adaptive depth" scale from 0 to 4. The fund names levels 1 and 2. OUR VIEW: it is asking for level 4.
25	
26	| Level | Examples in the notes | What the evidence shows |
27	|---|---|---|
28	| 0: uses no patient data | Nerivio migraine wearable, switched on by the patient, rated 0-1 [D1-02-F12]. India: none rated 0 | Nothing adapts. |
29	| 1: shows data | India: pocket ECGs (search summary only) [D1-04-F32]. Abroad: Omron VitalSight [D1-01-F39] | Self-monitoring alone: no effect [D1-01-F05]; one exception, a glucose sensor, in part D [D1-01-F42]. |
30	| 2: reminders, generic content | India: government Simple app, with overdue lists and reminder messages [D3-05-F03]. Abroad: Medisafe reminder app | Medisafe, 411 US adults, 12 weeks, against control: 0.5 mmHg, not significant [D1-01-F06]. |
31	| 3: coaching from the person's own data | India: Sugar.fit, BeatO, Fitterfly [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Abroad: CureApp HT, Japan | CureApp HT, 390 untreated patients, 12 weeks, against lifestyle advice alone: 24-hour systolic 2.4 mmHg lower [D1-01-F07]. |
32	| 4: changes the therapy (dose, protocol step, exercise prescription) | India: only Sanofi's My Dose Coach found, its Indian results unconfirmed [D1-04-F09]. Abroad: d-Nav; insulin pumps [D1-05-F41] | d-Nav dose device (maker-linked authors), 181 US insulin users, 6 months, against clinician support alone: HbA1c (three-month average sugar) down 1.0 point against 0.3 [D1-01-F13]. |
33	
34	**The line between 3 and 4.** Level 3 changes the advice: what to eat, how to exercise. Level 4 changes the prescription: a new dose or protocol step. A clinician approving each change keeps it at level 4. Indian diabetes programmes sit at 3: no page says sensor data changes a drug dose [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The test: after the software runs, the prescription is different.
35	
36	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: level 4 is the entry condition, however good the sensor.
37	
38	### B4. The loop: sense, decide, confirm, act, learn
39	
40	Five stages: what happens at each, and where existing products stop.
41	
42	![Monitoring against a therapy loop](adaptive-care-pictures/00-the-loop.png)
43	
44	*Diagram: monitoring stops at the reading; a therapy loop changes the treatment.*
45	
46	- **Sense.** A home device gives a number, valid only if taken correctly. Level 1 products stop here (B3).
47	- **Decide.** Software applies a written protocol to this patient's readings and proposes the next step. Coaching apps decide advice, not doses [D1-04-F04]; the protocol model of the government's Simple app stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step ladder was found in it [D1-06-F40].
48	- **Confirm.** A doctor, nurse or health worker approves each change; unsafe cases go to a specialist. Trials used pharmacists [D1-01-F04] or village doctors [D1-01-F09]; no Indian service doing this from home readings was found [D1-04-F09].
49	- **Act.** The patient gets the new dose, medicine or exercise level. Heart-failure telemonitoring trials without a mandated dose protocol found no benefit (B6).
50	- **Learn.** The next readings show whether it worked, and the loop runs again. At 24 government-programme sites, 10,621 of 21,895 patients did not return [D1-03-F10].
51	
52	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: India lacks decide, confirm and act between visits.
53	
54	### B5. A map of feedback-driven therapies
55	
56	Five kinds, by what the loop changes.
57	
58	| What changes | Home signal | How fast it responds | Proof | Who decides |
59	|---|---|---|---|---|
60	| 1. Drug dose or protocol step | Cuff, fasting sugar, INR (clotting test), weight | Days to weeks: insulin every 3 days in a 2025 US rule [D1-06-F16]; blood pressure re-checked at 30 days [D1-06-F14] | Strong: randomised trials with fewer deaths, clots or hospital stays [D1-01-F38, D1-01-F27, D1-02-F05] | Patient on an agreed plan, pharmacist, nurse or health worker [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04, D1-02-F06, D1-01-F09] |
61	| 2. Food and behaviour | Glucose sensor, step count | Each meal [D1-01-F22] | Mixed: a company-linked Indian trial cut HbA1c 2.9 points against 0.3 with standard care (319 people, 1 year) [D1-01-F19]; a US review of type 2 tools without a continuous sensor was negative (B7) [D1-01-F40] | App, coach |
62	| 3. Exercise as the dose | Camera, pulse, effort rating | Each session [D1-06-F36] | Matches in-person care; no better than usual care (pooled stroke trials, 661 people) [D1-02-F07] | Therapist or app [D1-02-F54] |
63	| 4. Therapy delivered by the device (closed-loop insulin pump) | Glucose sensor | Automatic | Strong: against a sensor alone, a dose algorithm cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points (319 adults with type 2 diabetes, US and Canada, 13 weeks, Tandem-funded) [D1-01-F43] | Algorithm, within clinician-set limits [D1-05-F41] |
64	| 5. Biofeedback (a body signal shown back to the patient) | Breathing or pulse sensor | During practice [D1-02-F15] | Weak: guided breathing had no blood-pressure effect once maker-linked trials were excluded (8 trials, 494 people) [D1-02-F11] | Patient |
65	
66	OUR VIEW: proof is strongest in kinds 1 and 4, where a drug dose with a known effect is changed and the signal is cheap, valid and fast. Kind 4 needs expensive hardware; kind 1 needs almost none. A student team, and a low-resource country, should start there.
67	
68	### B6. Five rules the evidence gives
69	
70	OUR VIEW: five rules, each with the numbers behind it.
71	
72	**1. The reading must change the treatment.** Across 15 pooled trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring alone lowered systolic pressure 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect; with intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling), not dose changes alone, 6.1 [D1-01-F05]. Two US heart-failure trials of remote monitoring without a mandated dose protocol (1,653 and 1,437 patients, 180 days) found no benefit [D1-01-F32, D1-01-F33]. Fast dose stepping after discharge cut readmission or death (B7) [D1-01-F27]. Against usual care, warfarin patients who set their own dose from home tests had fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.55, 8 trials); in 3 separate trials, those who left the dose to the clinic did not (0.94); the two approaches were not compared head to head [D1-02-F05].
73	
74	**2. Who is allowed to decide matters more than the electronics.** In a UK trial (1,182 patients, 12 months), sending readings electronically added a non-significant 1.2 mmHg over paper once the family doctor adjusted doses [D1-01-F03]. In rural China (33,995 people, 18 months), supervised village doctors stepping drugs by protocol got 57.0% under 130/80, against 19.9% with enhanced usual care [D1-01-F09]. At 4 years cardiovascular events were lower (hazard ratio 0.75 at age 60 and over), though the programme also gave free or discounted drugs and paid incentives [D1-01-F38].
75	
76	**The Indian null result belongs here.** mWellcare (40 community health centres, 3,698 people with hypertension or diabetes, 12 months, randomised by centre) gave nurses and doctors an app that prompted treatment steps. Against enhanced usual care the systolic difference was 0.98 mmHg, not significant; both arms fell about 13 mmHg [D1-01-F46]. OUR VIEW: it shows that a prompt at a visit adds nothing to a well-run programme. It does not show that dose changes between visits fail: no Indian randomised trial tested that (D1-01, NOT FOUND list).
77	
78	**3. Adherence technology alone does not move outcomes.** Smart pillboxes or medication labels for tuberculosis (23,483 patients, four countries) did not reduce poor outcomes against standard care [D1-02-F59]. Inhaler reminders for 220 New Zealand children gave 84% adherence against 30% over 6 months, with no difference in school absence [D1-02-F01]. OUR VIEW: raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, so adherence is an input to the dose decision, not a product.
79	
80	**4. Someone must pay for the outcome.** Apps and sensors sold on their own failed. Pear's assets fetched just over $6 million against $130 million of liabilities (2023-2024) [D1-02-F42]; Teva stopped US distribution of its sensor inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41]. Those at scale are paid by employers and insurers for clinician-led programmes (Hinge Health: revenue $234.970 million in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]) or sell a therapy device (Insulet: $842.0 million [D1-05-F41]).
81	
82	**5. People stay when their own clinician is in it.** In 8 remote US studies (over 1,00,000 participants) median retention was 5.5 days. Clinician referral added 40 days [D1-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: a consumer app is the wrong shape.
83	
84	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: B10 turns these rules into a test for any idea.
85	
86	### B7. What "measurable" means
87	
88	One endpoint per condition that a pilot could read at about 90 days.
89	
90	| Condition | Endpoint | Effect the trials found | "Clinically meaningful" threshold |
91	|---|---|---|---|
92	| High blood pressure | Share under 140/90 [D1-06-F03] | 57.2% controlled with pharmacist dose changes from home readings, against 30.0% with usual care (450 US patients, at both 6 and 12 months) [D1-01-F04] | 5 mmHg systolic against usual care [D1-01-F39] |
93	| Type 2 diabetes on insulin | HbA1c | Down 1.44-1.48 points with daily dose proposals, against 0.92 with standard care (191 adults, France, 4 months) [D1-01-F14] | None given; a US review judged 0.23-0.60 points not meaningful for type 2 tools without a continuous sensor [D1-05-F4] |
94	| Diabetes with a sensor | Time in range | Up 14 points with a dose algorithm (B5) [D1-01-F43] | NOT RESEARCHED |
95	| Heart failure | Readmission or death | 15.2% against 23.3% at 180 days with fast dose stepping after discharge (1,078 patients, 14 countries; adjusted estimates; side effects 41% against 29%) [D1-01-F27] | NOT RESEARCHED |
96	| Warfarin | Time in the target INR range | Trials against usual care report clots (risk ratio 0.47) and deaths (0.55) instead [D1-02-F05] | NOT RESEARCHED |
97	
98	No blood-pressure dose-change trial in our first-round notes reported before 6 months [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F04].
99	
100	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: for blood pressure, measure the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned.
101	
102	### B8. What "cannot access frequent specialist support" means in India
103	
104	Five numbers show the gap.
105	
106	1. **79.9%**: required posts in four specialities (surgery, medicine, obstetrics, paediatrics) unfilled at rural community health centres, March 2023 [D1-03-F16].
107	2. **About 650** endocrinologists and **4,000** cardiologists, 2017 count (search summary only) [D1-03-F18].
108	3. **About 2 minutes**: a primary-care consultation, 2013-2015 [D1-03-F24].
109	4. **51%**: of 21,895 patients at 24 government hypertension programme sites returned for follow-up, 2018-2019 [D1-03-F10].
110	5. **9.8%**: diabetes control rate in a Tamil Nadu survey (denominator not stated), though over 95% of diagnosed patients were on treatment (6,856 adults, 2025 paper) [D1-03-F09].
111	
112	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: the scarce thing is the prescriber's decision, which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make.
113	
114	### B9. Terms used in this document
115	
116	- **Adaptive depth:** 0-4 score for how far a product changes treatment.
117	- **Adherence:** taking the medicine as prescribed.
118	- **Closed loop:** a device that measures and adjusts therapy itself.
119	- **Digital therapeutic:** software that changes one patient's treatment.
120	- **Endpoint:** the result a trial is judged on.
121	- **Hazard ratio:** a risk ratio measured over time; below 1 means fewer events.
122	- **HbA1c:** blood test of average sugar over about three months.
123	- **INR:** clotting test that sets the warfarin dose.
124	- **Not significant:** small enough to be chance (a null result).
125	- **Protocol:** a written step-by-step treatment plan.
126	- **Randomised trial:** people get treatments by chance.
127	- **Risk ratio:** risk with treatment divided by risk without; below 1 means lower risk.
128	- **Systolic:** the upper blood-pressure number, in mmHg (millimetres of mercury).
129	- **Time in range:** share of the day with sugar at 70-180 mg/dL.
130	- **Titration:** stepping a dose towards a target.
131	
132	### B10. So what for us
133	
134	OUR VIEW. Any idea must pass three questions.
135	
136	1. **What changes?** After a home reading the prescription is different (level 4), within days.
137	2. **Who decides?** A general doctor, nurse or health worker, under a written protocol; unsafe cases go to a specialist.
138	3. **What moves, and who pays?** One endpoint passes an accepted threshold in 90 days, and a named payer wants it.
139	
140	![Same loop, new protocol](adaptive-care-pictures/15-same-loop-new-protocol.png)
141	
142	*Diagram: the same loop runs insulin, heart-failure and warfarin rules; only the home signal and the protocol file change.*
143

155	- All Indian tech start-ups raised US$7.2 billion in H1 2026, up 12%, with fewer deals (search summary only) [D2-05-F13].
156	
157	### 10. The rules in India
158	
159	These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO (the national medical-device regulator).
160	
161	**(a) Software as a medical device.** CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" (CDSCO/MD/GD/MDSW/01/2026) on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. Class follows the intended use, as stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. Its grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:
162	
163	| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
164	|---|---|---|---|
165	| Critical | D | C | B |
166	| Serious | C | B | A |
167	| Non-serious | B | A | A |
168	
169	"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" and support for "safe and effective use of medicinal products" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits, so the class turns on that grading [D2-04-F05]. A patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical" [D2-04-F03]. CDSCO names a hypertension digital therapeutics platform and a Bluetooth cuff app as medical device software, and bars the wellness carve-out once a disease is named [D2-04-F07, D2-04-F09]. Unlike the US, there is no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. CDSCO confirms the class on review [D2-04-F06].
170	
171	**(b) A study on patients before a licence.** A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14]; the flowchart notes it is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. A desk test on open data, simulators or teammates is not a clinical investigation; whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Fees and processing days NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].
172	
173	**(c) Telemedicine.** The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; such tools may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. List B medicines may be added at a follow-up; the guidelines define follow-up as the same doctor, same condition, within 6 months of the previous in-person consultation (clause 3.6.2) [D2-04-F17, D2-01-F10]. Annexure 1 names hypertension examples (List A refills such as enalapril and atenolol; List B add-on of a thiazide diuretic with atenolol); amlodipine, telmisartan and chlorthalidone are not named [D2-04-F17]. The claims check read the official text; whether later rules changed it in 2026 was not checked [D2-04-F17].
174	
175	**(d) Nurse or health officer changing a dose.** In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription"; no titration by them is described [D2-04-F18]. NOT FOUND: any law, rule or ministry order letting a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18].
176	
177	**(e) Claims and advertising.** The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats a disease in its Schedule, which lists "Diabetes", "Heart diseases" and "High or low blood pressure" [D2-04-F31]. Whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested; a question for counsel [D2-04-F31].
178	
179	**(f) Data law.** Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, consent-manager rules start one year after 13 Nov 2025, on 13 Nov 2026; notice, consent and data-fiduciary duties start 18 months after, on 13 May 2027, by the gazette's wording; one law firm (AZB) says a day earlier, 12 Nov 2026 and 12 May 2027 [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20]. Health data has no general exemption; only children's-data duties are waived for health providers [D2-04-F40].
180	
181	**(g) Ethics and registration.** ICMR's 2023 AI guidelines say humans should keep "complete control" and require consent that names the AI [D2-04-F35]. Trial registration on CTRI is mandatory before first enrolment for trials, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a clinician-decides pilot needs it is NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45].
182	
183	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.
184	
185	### 11. The rules and payment abroad
186	
187	Each country has a device route and a payment route; none fits our loop exactly.
188	
189	| | Device rule | How it is paid | NOT FOUND |
190	|---|---|---|---|
191	| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k): My Dose Coach (K163099, K171230), d-Nav (K181916) [D2-04-F24]. Software is not a device if it supports a clinician who can review its basis and does not analyse a device signal [D2-04-F22]; FDA's 6 Jan 2026 guidance extends this to a single recommendation, for clinician-facing tools only [D2-04-F23]. ## 4. The product we can build

Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end, in plain words: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols later.

### 4.1 What it does

OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who do not come back for the 30-day review (the half who do not return, chapter 1) [D1-03-F10]. Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects the step in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.

The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder, with a re-check after 30 days on each step [D1-06-F14]:

| Step | Medicine | What the sheet adds |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Amlodipine 5 mg | |
| 2 | Amlodipine 10 mg | "After 30 days measure BP again. If still high: Increase to Amlodipine 10mg" |
| 3 | Add telmisartan 40 mg | |
| 4 | Telmisartan 80 mg | Blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein are checked first. Any abnormal value: refer; if no specialist can be reached, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone |
| 5 | Add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg | Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available |
| After step 5 | | "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." |

The sheet covers adults over 30, asks for a compliance check at each visit before a dose is raised, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception [D1-06-F14].

### 4.2 The system map

A loop that changes treatment has six stages. For each one, open parts already exist; the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).

| Stage | Its job | Technology that exists | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sense | Get a number from the patient's home | Omron cuffs read with omblepy [D1-06-F07]; cuff-screen photo readers [D2-02-F4] | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
| Check the reading | Was it taken properly | AHA and ESH home rules [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11]; posture-error trials [D2-02-F16] | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed next step | Step protocols [D1-06-F14]; HL7 CQL [D2-03-F52]; OpenAPS bounds [D2-03-F46] | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | CDS Hooks cards with an accept button [D2-03-F53] | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram bot [D2-01-F9]; Indian speech services [D2-03-F58] | Telegram chat plus a web form |
| Learn | Improve choices from each patient's response | Personal drug-response trials [D2-03-F12]; adaptive message timing [D2-03-F10] | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |

![System map of the blood-pressure step loop from home reading to approved change](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)

*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*

The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It has no input or output, no clock and no randomness. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank (`null`), and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path (the reason is in chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F38]. A model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.

### 4.3 The patient side

![Phone chat in Hindi: the patient sends a photo of the cuff screen and next day receives the doctor's dose change](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The patient uses a Telegram chat; a web form does the same job if the chat fails. The chat prompts a measurement, takes a photo or a typed reading, asks two questions about tablets and delivers the change. The phone may be a family member's (chapter 1).

The home-reading rule (OUR DESIGN, from published guidance):

- **When:** days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle; two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the morning before tablets and in the evening [D2-01-F1, D2-02-F10].
- **A valid session:** both readings pass the quality checks; the session's value is their mean.
- **Enough readings:** at least 3 valid days, aiming for 7. The European Society of Hypertension (ESH) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-01-F1].
- **Still high:** a mean of 135 systolic or 85 diastolic or above. The ESH says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the International Society of Hypertension uses the same home line [D2-01-F3], and so do the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4].
- **Very high:** any single session at or above 180 systolic or 110 diastolic.

The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings ("SBP 140 or DBP 90") [D1-06-F14]. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a protocol value that the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

Every route writes the same record: systolic, diastolic, pulse, time, source and a quality flag. The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; the two reads must agree, and photos of the cuff's memory screen are rejected. This matters because purpose-trained photo readers do well on good images, field images are often poor, and general vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F4, D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; joining it by time to the clip's record (section 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built. Bluetooth is used only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].

### 4.4 The doctor side

![Doctor's queue of six proposals, each with the home average, the proposed action and Approve or Review buttons](adaptive-care-pictures/11-bp-doctor-queue.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The doctor sees a queue of cards, urgent ones first, batched once a day. Each card shows the current step, a 7-day sparkline (a small chart of the week's readings), the mean, the answer to the medicine question, the protocol line it quotes, the safety checks ticked and the proposed regimen, with Approve, Edit and Reject. A timer logs how long each decision takes. Because the card carries the readings, the protocol line and the checks, the decision is one tap (OUR DESIGN).

![One proposal card opened, with valid and rejected home readings, medicine taken, the protocol path, the reasons for the step and the safety checks](adaptive-care-pictures/12-bp-doctor-detail.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name. That is OUR DESIGN and a question for a lawyer, because India's telemedicine guidelines say the final prescription has to be delivered directly by the registered doctor (chapter 2.6) [D2-04-F17].

### 4.5 Trusting the reading

A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with the cuff, and the two largest posture mistakes have published sizes (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F16]. The loop answers this with a small clip built from the maker kit (OUR DESIGN). An ESP32 board carries two MPU6050 motion sensors, one on the cuff and one on the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once, and the clip stores that posture. Then it:

- enforces 300 seconds of still rest, restarting if the person moves;
- checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture;
- requires stillness through each 60-second measurement, and 60 seconds between readings;
- shows green or red and posts its reasons, joined to the reading by time.

A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2) [D2-02-F17]. The thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE. The clip does not measure blood pressure. What it cannot see (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, a full bladder, smoking) goes into a 4-question phone checklist.

![The reading-quality clip on the upper arm and forearm, with its green and red states](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)

*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*

Cuff size matters too: a regular cuff on a large arm reads high (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F19]. So the app asks the arm size and refuses arms outside the cuff's range; the Omron HEM-7120 standard cuff fits 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30]. The team uses cuffs on an independent validation list: the HEM-7120 passed ESH-IP 2010 [D2-02-F28], while the HEM-7156T's validation is Omron's own table (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-02-F29] and a popular Indian model is listed as not clinically validated [D2-02-F32].

OUR VIEW: the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.

### 4.6 Was the medicine taken

Raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, and adherence tools on their own did not move outcomes (chapter 2.1) [D1-02-F59]. So before any step-up the chat asks two questions, as buttons (OUR DESIGN):

- "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more"
- "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no"

Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number [D1-06-F14]. Any missed day, or no tablets left, sends support instead of a step-up, and a card goes to the clinician for information.

### 4.7 Safety built into the design

The engine runs its checks in a fixed order and proposes a step only at the end (OUR DESIGN, from the Gujarat sheet [D1-06-F14]):

| Order | Check | What the engine does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Patient referred or waiting for lab results | Nothing |
| 1 | Outside the sheet's population (30 or under), or diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease | Flags "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle |
| 2 | Readings that failed the quality gate | Drops them |
| 3 | Newest session at or above 180 or 110 | Asks for a repeat after rest; if confirmed, raises an urgent card and tells the patient to contact the clinic today. This beats the 30-day wait |
| 3 | Low readings | Fires only once a clinician sets the threshold, which the sheet does not give |
| 4 | Fewer than 3 valid days | Asks for more readings |
| 5 | Fewer than 30 days on the step | "Keep going" |
| 6 | Home mean below 135/85 | "Same medicine"; no doctor needed |
| 7 | At or above the line | Asks the medicine question (section 4.6) |
| 8 | Already on the last step | Proposes referral |
| 9 | Pregnancy, or a woman of childbearing age not on effective contraception, and the next step has a barred drug | Proposes referral; amlodipine steps may go ahead; uncontrolled on the higher amlodipine dose: referral |
| 9 | Lab values missing before telmisartan 80 mg; any value abnormal | Proposes a lab order; for an abnormal value, referral, or, with no specialist reachable, withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone |
| 10 | None of the above | Proposes the next step, quoting the sheet line |

The very-high action is OUR DESIGN for home readings; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry [D1-06-F14]. Like other working dose algorithms, the engine only chooses written regimens, holds the current step when data is missing, and never steps on one reading (chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F46].

OUR VIEW: four things are never dropped. They are valid home readings; the medicine-taken check; a proposal true to the protocol, with its reasons and safety branches; and a doctor's approval of every change. Two things are ruled out for good: a dose worked out outside the protocol file, and a language model in the dose path.

### 4.8 Same loop, new protocol

OUR VIEW: each new protocol is a new market on the same engine, approval screen and safety method. The engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.

| Order | Protocol | Home signal | Rule in the notes | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | High blood pressure | Cuff | Gujarat's ladder [D1-06-F14]; a Nigerian ladder as a second file [D1-06-F15] | Being built tonight |
| 2 | Insulin, then the tablet steps for diabetes | Sugar meter | "increase 2 units every 3 days" [D1-06-F16] | On paper only |
| 3 | Heart failure | Weight, pressure, pulse, lab values | Step up to full doses soon after discharge [D1-01-F27] | Roadmap; needs a diagnostics partner |
| 4 | Warfarin, then asthma | INR meter; inhaler use | Dosing tables differ between sources (search summary only) [D1-06-F37] | Roadmap |

![Table of four protocols that share one loop: blood pressure now, insulin next, heart failure and warfarin later](adaptive-care-pictures/15-same-loop-new-protocol.png)

*Diagram: the engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.*

The picture says a "doctor or health worker" approves. That is the later aim, not tonight's design. Only a registered doctor may prescribe under the telemedicine guidelines (section 4.4), and no Indian rule was found that lets a nurse or health officer change a dose (chapter 2.6) [D2-04-F18]. It remains a question for counsel.

Full detail: Appendix C (the technology behind each stage, reading quality and the protocol as data) and Appendix G (the protocol file, the decision steps and the screens).

OUR VIEW: the product is simple on purpose. The rules are the state's own; the hard parts are a reading that can be trusted, the choice between stepping up and supporting, and a doctor who stays in control. A product like this is worth building only if a small version of it can be built and tested honestly in one night. Chapter 5 shows that version, rung by rung.

- checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture;
- requires stillness through each 60-second measurement, and 60 seconds between readings;
- shows green or red and posts its reasons, joined to the reading by time.

A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2) [D2-02-F17]. The thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE. The clip does not measure blood pressure. What it cannot see (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, a full bladder, smoking) goes into a 4-question phone checklist.

![The reading-quality clip on the upper arm and forearm, with its green and red states](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)

*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*

Cuff size matters too: a regular cuff on a large arm reads high (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F19]. So the app asks the arm size and refuses arms outside the cuff's range; the Omron HEM-7120 standard cuff fits 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30]. The team uses cuffs on an independent validation list: the HEM-7120 passed ESH-IP 2010 [D2-02-F28], while the HEM-7156T's validation is Omron's own table (THEIR CLAIM) [D2-02-F29] and a popular Indian model is listed as not clinically validated [D2-02-F32].

OUR VIEW: the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.

### 4.6 Was the medicine taken

Raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, and adherence tools on their own did not move outcomes (chapter 2.1) [D1-02-F59]. So before any step-up the chat asks two questions, as buttons (OUR DESIGN):

- "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more"
- "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no"

Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number [D1-06-F14]. Any missed day, or no tablets left, sends support instead of a step-up, and a card goes to the clinician for information.

### 4.7 Safety built into the design

The engine runs its checks in a fixed order and proposes a step only at the end (OUR DESIGN, from the Gujarat sheet [D1-06-F14]):

| Order | Check | What the engine does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Patient referred or waiting for lab results | Nothing |
| 1 | Outside the sheet's population (30 or under), or diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease | Flags "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle |
| 2 | Readings that failed the quality gate | Drops them |
| 3 | Newest session at or above 180 or 110 | Asks for a repeat after rest; if confirmed, raises an urgent card and tells the patient to contact the clinic today. This beats the 30-day wait |
| 3 | Low readings | Fires only once a clinician sets the threshold, which the sheet does not give |
| 4 | Fewer than 3 valid days | Asks for more readings |
| 5 | Fewer than 30 days on the step | "Keep going" |
| 6 | Home mean below 135/85 | "Same medicine"; no doctor needed |
| 7 | At or above the line | Asks the medicine question (section 4.6) |
| 8 | Already on the last step | Proposes referral |
| 9 | Pregnancy, or a woman of childbearing age not on effective contraception, and the next step has a barred drug | Proposes referral; amlodipine steps may go ahead; uncontrolled on the higher amlodipine dose: referral |
| 9 | Lab values missing before telmisartan 80 mg; any value abnormal | Proposes a lab order; for an abnormal value, referral, or, with no specialist reachable, withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone |
| 10 | None of the above | Proposes the next step, quoting the sheet line |

The very-high action is OUR DESIGN for home readings; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry [D1-06-F14]. Like other working dose algorithms, the engine only chooses written regimens, holds the current step when data is missing, and never steps on one reading (chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F46].

OUR VIEW: four things are never dropped. They are valid home readings; the medicine-taken check; a proposal true to the protocol, with its reasons and safety branches; and a doctor's approval of every change. Two things are ruled out for good: a dose worked out outside the protocol file, and a language model in the dose path.

### 4.8 Same loop, new protocol

OUR VIEW: each new protocol is a new market on the same engine, approval screen and safety method. The engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.

| Order | Protocol | Home signal | Rule in the notes | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | High blood pressure | Cuff | Gujarat's ladder [D1-06-F14]; a Nigerian ladder as a second file [D1-06-F15] | Being built tonight |
| 2 | Insulin, then the tablet steps for diabetes | Sugar meter | "increase 2 units every 3 days" [D1-06-F16] | On paper only |
| 3 | Heart failure | Weight, pressure, pulse, lab values | Step up to full doses soon after discharge [D1-01-F27] | Roadmap; needs a diagnostics partner |
| 4 | Warfarin, then asthma | INR meter; inhaler use | Dosing tables differ between sources (search summary only) [D1-06-F37] | Roadmap |

![Table of four protocols that share one loop: blood pressure now, insulin next, heart failure and warfarin later](adaptive-care-pictures/15-same-loop-new-protocol.png)

*Diagram: the engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.*

The picture says a "doctor or health worker" approves. That is the later aim, not tonight's design. Only a registered doctor may prescribe under the telemedicine guidelines (section 4.4), and no Indian rule was found that lets a nurse or health officer change a dose (chapter 2.6) [D2-04-F18]. It remains a question for counsel.

Full detail: Appendix C (the technology behind each stage, reading quality and the protocol as data) and Appendix G (the protocol file, the decision steps and the screens).

OUR VIEW: the product is simple on purpose. The rules are the state's own; the hard parts are a reading that can be trusted, the choice between stepping up and supporting, and a doctor who stays in control. A product like this is worth building only if a small version of it can be built and tested honestly in one night. Chapter 5 shows that version, rung by rung.

"""Checks on the joined report. Run after join_parts.py and link_facts.py.

Usage:  python check_report.py <report.md> [--links]

Reports
- banned words, em dashes, exclamation marks
- picture links that point to a missing file
- paragraphs and table rows that contain a number but no fact link and no tag
  (OUR ARITHMETIC, OUR ESTIMATE, OUR VIEW, ASSUMPTION, EXAMPLE, THEIR CLAIM, NOT RESEARCHED...)
- with --links: every distinct source URL is requested once and failures are listed
"""
import re
import sys
import urllib.request
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

if hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure"):
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")

BANNED = [
    "synergy", "revolutionary", "game-changing", "ai-powered", "seamless", "leverage", "utilise", "utilize",
    "robust", "cutting-edge", "innovative", "streamline", "optimise", "optimize", "empower", "unlock",
    "world-class", "best-in-class", "next-gen", "ecosystem", "holistic", "delve", "landscape",
]
TAGS = ("OUR ARITHMETIC", "OUR ESTIMATE", "OUR VIEW", "ASSUMPTION", "EXAMPLE", "THEIR CLAIM", "NOT RESEARCHED",
        "NOT FOUND", "OUR DESIGN", "OUR SIMULATION", "Mock-up", "TARGET")
FACT_LINK = re.compile(r"\[D\d-\d\d-F\d+\]\(|D\d-\d\d-F\d+")
NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z#/-])\d[\d,.]*\s?(%|mmHg|crore|lakh|million|billion|patients|people|points)|[₹$£€]\s?\d")


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
    report = Path(sys.argv[1])
    text = report.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    lines = text.splitlines()
    problems = 0

    print("== words and marks")
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if line.startswith(">") or "THEIR CLAIM" in line:
            continue
        low = re.sub(r"\]\([^)]*\)", "]", line.lower())
        low = re.sub(r"\"[^\"]*\"", "", low)
        for w in BANNED:
            if re.search(r"(?<![a-z-])" + re.escape(w) + r"(?![a-z])", low):
                print("  line %d: banned word '%s'" % (i, w))
                problems += 1
        if "—" in line:
            print("  line %d: em dash" % i)
            problems += 1
        if re.search(r"[a-z]!(\s|$)", line) and not line.lstrip().startswith("!["):
            print("  line %d: exclamation mark" % i)
            problems += 1

    print("== pictures")
    for m in re.finditer(r"!\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)", text):
        p = report.parent / m.group(1)
        if not p.exists():
            print("  missing picture: " + m.group(1))
            problems += 1

    print("== numbers without a source or a tag")
    untagged, in_code, section = 0, False, ""
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, 1):
        if line.startswith("```"):
            in_code = not in_code
        if in_code:
            continue
        if line.startswith("#"):
            section = line.strip("# ").strip()
            continue
        if line.startswith("|---") or line.startswith("![") or not line.strip():
            continue
        if NUMBER.search(line) and not FACT_LINK.search(line) and not any(t in line for t in TAGS):
            untagged += 1
            if untagged <= 60:
                print("  line %d [%s]: %s" % (i, section[:28], line.strip()[:120]))
    print("  total lines with a number and no source or tag: %d" % untagged)

Usage:  python check_restructure.py <old_parts_dir> <new_parts_dir>

Reports
- fact IDs cited in the old parts but missing from the new parts, and IDs that are new
- numbers in the new text that appear nowhere in the old text (to check by hand)
- old-style cross-references left in the new text ("part F2", "tab H", "Decision brief")
- pictures: each should be placed exactly once
- story repetition: how often the most-repeated old facts are cited in the story chapters
- word counts per new part
"""
import collections
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

if hasattr(sys.stdout, "reconfigure"):
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")

FULL = re.compile(r"D(\d)-(\d\d)-F0*(\d+)")
SHORT = re.compile(r"(D\d-\d\d)-F0*\d+((?:\s*(?:,|and|to)\s*F0*\d+)+)")
URL = re.compile(r"https?://\S+")
PIC = re.compile(r"!\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)")
NUM = re.compile(r"(?<![\w.-])\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?")
STALE = re.compile(r"\b[Pp]arts? [A-M](?:\d|\b)|\b[Tt]ab [A-M]\b|\bDecision brief\b|\bsee [A-M]\d\b|\b(?:B|C|D|E|F|G)\d{1,2}\b(?! *\.)")
STORY = ("10", "20", "30", "40", "50", "60")


def ids(text):
    out = collections.Counter()
    for m in FULL.finditer(text):
        out["D%s-%s-F%d" % (m.group(1), m.group(2), int(m.group(3)))] += 1
    for m in SHORT.finditer(text):
        for n in re.findall(r"F0*(\d+)", m.group(2)):
            out["%s-F%d" % (m.group(1), int(n))] += 1
    return out


def numbers(text):
    text = URL.sub(" ", text)
    text = PIC.sub(" ", text)
    text = FULL.sub(" ", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\bF0*\d+\b", " ", text)
    return set(m.group(0).rstrip(",.") for m in NUM.finditer(text))


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        raise SystemExit(__doc__)
    old_dir, new_dir = Path(sys.argv[1]), Path(sys.argv[2])
    old_parts = {p.name: p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in sorted(old_dir.glob("*.md"))}
    new_parts = {p.name: p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in sorted(new_dir.glob("*.md"))}
    old_all, new_all = "\n".join(old_parts.values()), "\n".join(new_parts.values())
    problems = 0

    print("== fact IDs: %d in old, %d in new" % (len(old_ids), len(new_ids)))
    missing, extra = sorted(old_ids - new_ids), sorted(new_ids - old_ids)
    for label, group in (("missing from new", missing), ("new, not in old", extra)):

## 4. The product we can build

Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end, in plain words: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols later.

### 4.1 What it does

OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who do not come back for the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects the step in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.

The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (or hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." The sheet covers adults over 30, asks for a compliance check at each visit before a dose is raised, wants blood tests before telmisartan goes to 80 mg, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception. Every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].

### 4.2 The system map

A loop that changes treatment has six stages. For each one, open parts already exist (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).

| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|
| Sense | Get a number from the patient's home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
| Check the reading | Was it taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed next step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
| Learn | Improve choices from each patient's response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |

![System map of the blood-pressure step loop from home reading to approved change](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)

*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*

The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It has no clock and no randomness. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path, for the reason given in chapter 2.3. A model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.

### 4.3 The patient side

![Phone chat in Hindi: the patient sends a photo of the cuff screen and next day receives the doctor's dose change](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, often on a family member's phone (chapter 1). The chat prompts a measurement, takes a photo or a typed reading, asks two questions about tablets and delivers the change.

The home-reading rule is OUR DESIGN, built from published guidance. On days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the morning before tablets and in the evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks, and its value is their mean. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7; the European Society of Hypertension (ESH) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)", and that a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]. So the block is "still high" at a mean of 135 systolic or 85 diastolic or above, the home line the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] also use. Any single session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".

The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a protocol value that the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

Every route writes the same record: systolic, diastolic, pulse, time, source and a quality flag. ## 4. The product we can build

Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end, in plain words: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols later.

### 4.1 What it does

OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who do not come back for the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects it in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.

The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." It covers adults over 30, asks for a compliance check before a dose is raised, wants blood tests before telmisartan goes to 80 mg, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception. Every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].

### 4.2 The system map

A loop that changes treatment has six stages. Open parts already exist for each (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).

| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|
| Sense | Get a number from the home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
| Check | Was the reading taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
| Learn | Improve choices from each response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |

![System map of the step loop](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)

*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*

The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It has no clock and no randomness. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path, for the reason given in chapter 2.3. A model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.

### 4.3 The patient side

![Patient chat on the phone](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, often on a family member's phone (chapter 1). The chat prompts a measurement, takes a photo or a typed reading, asks two questions about tablets and delivers the change.

The home-reading rule is OUR DESIGN, built from published guidance. On days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the morning before tablets and in the evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks; its value is their mean. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7. The European Society of Hypertension (ESH) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)", and that a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]. So the block is "still high" at a mean of 135 systolic or 85 diastolic or above, the home line that the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] also use. A single session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".

The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a protocol value that the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; the two reads must agree, and photos of the cuff's memory screen are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; joining it by time to the clip's record (section 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built. Bluetooth is used only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].

### 4.4 The doctor side

![Clinician queue of proposal cards](adaptive-care-pictures/11-bp-doctor-queue.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The doctor sees a queue of cards, urgent ones first, batched once a day. Each card shows the current step, a 7-day sparkline (a small chart of the week's readings), the mean, the answer to the medicine question, the protocol line it quotes, the safety checks ticked and the proposed regimen, with Approve, Edit and Reject. A timer logs how long each decision takes. Because the card carries the readings, the line and the checks, the decision is one tap (OUR DESIGN).

![One proposal card in detail](adaptive-care-pictures/12-bp-doctor-detail.png)

*Mock-up with example data.*

The approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name. That is OUR DESIGN and a question for a lawyer, because India's telemedicine guidelines want the final prescription delivered directly by the registered doctor (chapter 2.6).

The home-reading rule is OUR DESIGN, built from published guidance. On days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, in the morning before tablets and in the evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks; its value is their mean. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7. The European Society of Hypertension (ESH) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)", and that a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]. So the block is "still high" at a mean of 135 systolic or 85 diastolic or above, the home line that the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] also use. A single session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".

The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a protocol value that the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; the two reads must agree, and photos of the cuff's memory screen are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; joining it by time to the clip's record (section 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built. Bluetooth is used only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].

This home action is OUR DESIGN; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry. A low-pressure rule acts only once a clinician sets its threshold, which the sheet does not give.

5. At or above the line: ask the medicine question (section 4.6).
6. The guards: referral after the last step; referral when pregnancy, or childbearing age without effective contraception, meets a barred drug (amlodipine steps may go ahead); a lab order before telmisartan 80 mg, and for an abnormal value, referral or, with no specialist reachable, withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone.
7. Only then: propose the next step, quoting the sheet line.

Like other working dose algorithms, the engine only chooses written regimens, holds the current step when data is missing and never steps on one reading (chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F46].

OUR VIEW: four things are never dropped: valid home readings; the medicine-taken check; a proposal true to the protocol, with its reasons and safety branches; and a doctor's approval of every change. Two things are ruled out for good: a dose worked out outside the protocol file, and a language model in the dose path.

The loop answers with a small clip built from the maker kit (OUR DESIGN): an ESP32 board with two MPU6050 motion sensors, one on the cuff and one on the forearm. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest, restarting if the person moves; checks that the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture; and requires stillness through each 60-second measurement. It shows green or red and posts its reasons, joined to the reading by time.
