content.content:
1	## 4. The product we can build
2	
3	Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols.
4	
5	### 4.1 What it does
6	
7	OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who do not come back for the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects it in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.
8	
9	The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." It covers adults over 30. Its safety rules are in section 4.7, and every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].
10	
11	### 4.2 The system map
12	
13	A loop that changes treatment has six stages. Open parts already exist for each (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).
14	
15	| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| Sense | Get a number from the home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
18	| Check | Was the reading taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
19	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
20	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
21	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
22	| Learn | Improve choices from each response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |
23	
24	![System map of the step loop](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)
25	
26	*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*
27	
28	The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path (chapter 2.3 gives the reason); a model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.
29	
30	### 4.3 The patient side
31	
32	![Patient chat on the phone](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)
33	
34	*Mock-up with example data.*
35	
36	The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, often on a family member's phone (chapter 1). The chat prompts a measurement, takes a photo or a typed reading, asks two questions about tablets and delivers the change.
37	
38	The home-reading rule is OUR DESIGN, built from published guidance. On days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7. The European Society of Hypertension says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)", and that a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use the same home line. So a mean at or above 135 systolic or 85 diastolic is "still high"; one session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".
39	
40	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.
41	
42	The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; memory screens are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; the clip's time-stamped record (section 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built; Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].
43	
44	### 4.4 The doctor side
45	
46	![Clinician queue of proposal cards](adaptive-care-pictures/11-bp-doctor-queue.png)
47	
48	*Mock-up with example data.*
49	
50	The doctor sees a queue of cards, urgent ones first, batched once a day. Each card shows the current step, a 7-day sparkline (a small chart of the week's readings), the mean, the answer to the medicine question, the protocol line it quotes, the safety checks ticked and the proposed regimen, with Approve, Edit and Reject. A timer logs each decision. Because the card carries everything needed, the decision is one tap (OUR DESIGN).
51	
52	![One proposal card in detail](adaptive-care-pictures/12-bp-doctor-detail.png)
53	
54	*Mock-up with example data.*
55	
56	The approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name. That is OUR DESIGN and a question for a lawyer, because India's telemedicine guidelines want the final prescription delivered directly by the registered doctor (chapter 2.6).
57	
58	### 4.5 Trusting the reading
59	
60	A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with the cuff; an arm hanging at the side or resting on the lap has a published effect (chapter 2.3). The loop answers with a small clip built from the maker kit (OUR DESIGN): an ESP32 board with two MPU6050 motion sensors, one on the cuff and one on the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once, and the clip stores that posture. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest, restarting on movement; checks that the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture; and requires stillness through each 60-second measurement. It shows green or red, with reasons, time-stamped to join the reading. A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2) [D2-02-F17]. The thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE. What the clip cannot see (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, a full bladder, smoking) goes into a 4-question phone checklist.
61	
62	![The reading-quality clip](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)
63	
64	*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*
65	
66	Cuff size matters too: a regular cuff on a large arm reads high [D2-02-F19]. So the app asks the arm size and refuses arms outside the cuff's range; the Omron HEM-7120 standard cuff fits 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30], and it passed an independent validation (ESH-IP 2010) [D2-02-F28].
67	
68	OUR VIEW: the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.
69	
70	### 4.6 Was the medicine taken
71	
72	Raising a dose that is not being taken is unsafe, and adherence tools on their own did not move outcomes (chapter 2.1). So before any step-up the chat asks two questions, as buttons (OUR DESIGN):
73	
74	- "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more"
75	- "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no"
76	
77	Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number. Any missed day, or no tablets left, sends support instead of a step-up, and a card goes to the clinician for information.
78	
79	### 4.7 Safety built into the design
80	
81	The engine runs its checks in a fixed order and proposes a step only at the end (OUR DESIGN, from the sheet):
82	
83	1. A patient who is referred or waiting for lab results is left alone. A patient aged 30 or under, or with diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease, is flagged "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle.
84	2. Readings that failed the quality gate are dropped.
85	3. Safety first. A session at or above 180 or 110 brings a request to repeat after rest; if confirmed, an urgent card goes to the doctor and the patient is told to contact the clinic today, ahead of the 30-day wait. This home action is OUR DESIGN; the sheet's 180/110 line is for clinic entry. A low-pressure rule acts only once a clinician sets its threshold.
86	4. Fewer than 3 valid days: ask for more. Under 30 days on the step: "keep going". Home mean below 135/85: "same medicine", no doctor needed.
87	5. At or above the line: the medicine question (section 4.6).
88	6. The guards: referral after the last step; referral when pregnancy, or childbearing age without effective contraception, meets a barred drug (amlodipine steps may go ahead); a lab order before telmisartan 80 mg, and for an abnormal value, referral or, with no specialist reachable, withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone.
89	7. Only then: propose the next step, quoting the sheet line.
90	
91	Like other working dose algorithms, the engine only chooses written regimens, holds the current step when data is missing and never steps on one reading (chapter 2.3) [D2-03-F46].
92	
93	OUR VIEW: four things are never dropped: valid home readings, the medicine-taken check, a protocol-true proposal with its reasons and safety branches, and a doctor's approval of every change. A dose worked out outside the protocol file, and a language model in the dose path, are ruled out for good.
94	
95	### 4.8 Same loop, new protocol
96	
97	OUR VIEW: each new protocol is a new market on the same engine, approval screen and safety method.
98	
99	| Order | Protocol | Home signal | Rule in the notes | Status |
100	|---|---|---|---|---|
101	| 1 | High blood pressure | Cuff | Gujarat's ladder; a Nigerian ladder as a second file [D1-06-F15] | Being built tonight |
102	| 2 | Insulin, then the tablet steps for diabetes | Sugar meter | "increase 2 units every 3 days" [D1-06-F16] | On paper only |
103	| 3 | Heart failure | Weight, pressure, pulse, lab values | Step up to full doses soon after discharge (chapter 2.1) | Roadmap; needs a diagnostics partner |
104	| 4 | Warfarin, then asthma | INR meter; inhaler use | Dosing tables differ between sources (search summary only) [D1-06-F37] | Roadmap |
105	
106	![Same loop, new protocol](adaptive-care-pictures/15-same-loop-new-protocol.png)
107	
108	*Diagram: the engine, the approval screen and the chat stay the same; only the home signal and the protocol file change.*
109	
110	The picture says a "doctor or health worker" approves. That is the later aim: only a registered doctor may prescribe (section 4.4), and no Indian rule was found that lets a nurse or health officer change a dose (chapter 2.6). It remains a question for counsel.
111	
112	Full detail: Appendix C (the technology behind each stage, reading quality, the protocol as data) and Appendix G (the protocol file, the decision steps, the screens).
113	
114	OUR VIEW: the product is simple on purpose. The rules are the state's own; the hard parts are a reading that can be trusted, the choice between stepping up and supporting, and a doctor who stays in control. Chapter 5 shows the smallest version that can be built and tested honestly in one night, and the steps after it.

## 5. The MVP

Chapter 4 showed the whole product. This chapter shows the MVP (minimum viable product: the smallest product that tests the business): what can be built and tested between 23:00 on Thursday 13 November and noon on Friday 14 November, what it can honestly prove, and the two rungs that follow it.

### 5.1 The ladder

OUR DESIGN, all three rungs:

| Rung | When | What it is | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Tonight | 23:00 Thu 13 Nov to 12:00 Fri 14 Nov | Engine, three screens, reading route, quality clip, tests, simulation | The code does what the protocol sheet says in every listed branch; readings flow end to end; a person can rule on a card in seconds | Anything about patients |
| 2. Two-week test | After the event | One clinic, a few patients already on step 1 or 2, their own doctor rules on every proposal | Patients send valid readings and doctors act on proposals inside normal work | Any change in blood pressure control |
| 3. 90-day pilot | After rung 2 and approvals | Several clinics, a comparison group | Whether more enrolled patients are under the home line at 90 days | Heart attacks, strokes, deaths |

OUR VIEW: each rung earns the next. Going to rung 3 without rung 2 would put an untried loop in front of an ethics committee.

### 5.2 Rung 1: what gets built tonight

OUR DESIGN, from the software and hardware build notes:

- **Software.** The `decide()` engine (chapter 4.2), in Python 3.11 with FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic and pytest. Three screens: the patient chat, the clinician queue, and a results page with the tests, coverage, the simulation chart, live-run counts, approve times and a dropdown to switch protocol.
- **Hardware.** The photo route and typed entry (chapter 4.3); Bluetooth through the omblepy tool only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand by about 02:00; the quality clip (chapter 4.5). A pill-box sensor is a stretch goal; a phone "taken" tap is the default. Cash outlay for one non-Bluetooth cuff and small parts is about ₹2,000-2,600 (OUR ARITHMETIC). Night delivery to Sonipat was not confirmed.
- **Protocol files.** The biology student owns them: Gujarat; Nigeria's losartan ladder as a second file, which covers adults 18 and over and has no lab check and no medicine-taken question [D1-06-F15]; and the American Diabetes Association's basal-insulin rule, on paper only, never run on a person. The claims check found four rules missing from the first Gujarat file (the age rule, the wider pregnancy rule, the abnormal-lab branch and the out-of-scope flag); they are now added.
- **Tests.** Thirty-six tests, one per listed branch, across both protocols and the insulin file. Four groups are still "to add", for the rules the claims check found: childbearing age, abnormal lab, outside the demo, and the Nigeria rules. Coverage target: every key in each file read by at least one test, plus line and branch coverage of `decide()`.
- **Team.** Six roles: E engine and I interfaces (computer science), P protocol and tests (biology), H1 clip and H2 cuff and photo route (hardware), L lead, story and simulation.
- **Checkpoints.** 02:00: a typed reading flows to a proposal, an approval and a message. 05:00: engine frozen. 09:30: testing stops; first dress rehearsal. 10:30: backup video recorded.
- **Cut lines.** If behind, drop in this order: WhatsApp; a third language; 20-seed simulation bands; the insulin file as tests (show the file only); Nigeria as a live dropdown (keep its tests); Telegram (use the web form); the photo or Bluetooth route (use typed readings). If the 02:00 checkpoint is missed, the first four go at once. Hardware falls back to one forearm sensor, no Bluetooth, and a phone tap for "taken".
- **Never cut:** the adherence check, the clinician approval step, the pregnancy and childbearing-age branch, the abnormal-lab branch, the "outside the demo" flag, the very-high branch, the test table and the safety statement.

The hardware is tested on 6 to 10 teammates, about 25 minutes each (OUR ESTIMATE). Volunteers agree verbally and are recorded by ID only; anyone at or above 180/110 is told to see a doctor and is not tested further. Each person is measured in correct posture, with the arm hanging at the side and with the arm on the lap, in coin-flip order, two readings each. The team reports counts and ranges, not p-values, and every failed photo and false alarm. This tests the pipeline and the clip, not cuff accuracy or patients.

OUR VIEW: the critical path is the schema, `decide()`, the first 29 tests, the queue with Approve, and the change message. Hardware hangs off it with a typed fallback, so a hardware failure costs a result, not the demo.

### 5.3 Honest tonight against roadmap

OUR VIEW.

| Tonight: built and tested by noon | Roadmap: needs patients, months or a partner |
|---|---|
| Protocol files for Gujarat and Nigeria, plus the insulin rule as paper only | A model of each patient's response to the next step, from real approved steps |
| A pure decision engine with every branch tested and coverage reported | Learning when to send each person a reminder, to complete reading blocks |
| Photo reading of any cuff with checks and patient confirmation; Bluetooth only if the cuff is in hand | A weighted reading-quality score instead of pass or fail |
| The quality clip on teammates: correct posture against arm at the side and on the lap | Insulin and heart-failure protocols in the same engine; heart failure needs lab values |
| Clinician approval queue and a Telegram patient chat | Indian-language voice and offline speech models |
| Replay on open home readings and a labelled simulated cohort | Cuffless sensing, only after a validation protocol exists |

### 5.4 The four results the team can show honestly

These are the only results that will exist by noon, with what each may and may not claim.

| Result | What is measured | May claim | May not claim |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) Branch coverage | Tests passing (target 36 of 36), line and branch coverage, protocol keys read | "The code does what the sheet says in every branch we listed" | "Safe", "clinically validated" |
| (ii) Simulated cohort | Control by month, needless step-ups, doctor workload | "Under stated assumptions, our model suggests..." | Any effect on patients |
| (iii) Live readings and clip | Readings received, share passing the gate, photo-to-stored time, photo accuracy, clip flags | "The pipeline works on real cuffs and real people" | Clinical data; that the clip improves control |
| (iv) Time to approve | Seconds per card and wrong taps, 3 people x 10 cards (OUR DESIGN) | "A person can rule on a card in about n seconds" | Clinical judgement; these are not clinicians on real patients |

Teammates' readings will mostly give "same medicine"; the step path is shown with a labelled synthetic patient.

**The simulated cohort** (OUR SIMULATION, not a trial, no effect on patients) follows 5,000 patients per arm for 12 monthly cycles. Each patient has a hidden step at which they would be controlled, set from the government programme's Punjab control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04]. 48% are non-adherent (search summary only; definition-dependent) [D1-03-F44], which is used only to count needless step-ups. The clinic arm attends each month at the return rate of chapter 1, an ASSUMPTION that favours the clinic arm. The loop arm sends a valid block in 30%, 50% or 70% of months (ASSUMPTION). In the first run (seed 1; to be re-run tonight, not to be quoted as data), control at month 12 was 39.0% in the clinic-only arm and 49.1%, 55.0% and 59.8% in the loop arm at those three engagement levels (OUR SIMULATION).

The build note's own reading: almost all the modelled gain comes from contact and refills, not from smarter stepping, because the step curve is flat after step 3; the adherence check mainly cuts needless step-ups. Both follow from the assumptions. The clinic arm's 39% (OUR SIMULATION) sits between district control and control among returners (chapter 1): plausible, not a validation. OUR VIEW: say the simulation's own finding aloud. "The gain comes from contact" is more credible than a dosing claim.

### 5.5 The 3-minute demo script

OUR DESIGN, from the software build note:

| Time | Who | On screen | Words |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00-0:25 | Lead | The programme's return and control figures (chapter 1) | "India's protocol works when patients come back. Half don't. We bring the 30-day visit home." |
| 0:25-0:50 | Lead | Loop diagram | "Reading in, protocol step out, doctor taps once, patient told in Hindi." |
| 0:50-1:30 | Patient teammate | Telegram: live cuff photo (or the clip); "2 good readings saved" | "Real reading, quality-checked." |
| 1:30-1:50 | Engine owner | Synthetic patient "Asha", 7 days near 148/92 on amlodipine 5 mg; adherence question, tap "0 days missed" | "Before stepping up, the protocol says check compliance. We ask." |
| 1:50-2:15 | Doctor (mentor or teammate) | Queue card with mean, readings, sheet line, guards; tap Approve; timer | "One tap. Every change is approved." |
| 2:15-2:30 | Patient teammate | Hindi message with the change and the doctor's name | "Change delivered in her language." |
| 2:30-2:50 | Biology student | Results page: 36 tests, coverage, simulation chart | "Every branch of the sheet tested. Our simulation, not a trial." |
| 2:50-3:00 | Lead | Switch the protocol to Nigeria; Asha's proposal becomes losartan 50 | "Same engine, any state's protocol." |

Backup: the whole flow on the local web page, plus the 10:30 recording. Asha's synthetic record must say she is past childbearing age (OUR DESIGN); otherwise both sheets' pregnancy rules block the telmisartan and losartan steps.

### 5.6 The safety statement

Shown on the first slide and in the README, word for word from the software build note:

> This is a student prototype built overnight. It is not medical advice and not a medical device. It does not diagnose or treat anyone. A clinician must approve every change of medicine; the software only drafts proposals from a published protocol. No patient data were used tonight. The readings shown are from teammates who volunteered and from synthetic patients; they are not clinical data. The simulation is our own model with stated assumptions, not a trial. Low-blood-pressure and lab-recency limits are deliberately left unset and must be set by a supervising clinician before any real use.

A one-page draft Deep Tech Thesis, already corrected with the claims-check wording and with three blanks for tonight's numbers, is in Appendix G, with six hard questions a deep-tech fund may ask about the software and hardware.

### 5.7 Rung 2: two weeks with a doctor in the loop

OUR DESIGN. It asks whether the loop survives normal clinic work, not whether it lowers pressure.

- **Setting:** one clinic; a small number of adults already on step 1 or 2; their own doctor reviews every proposal in a normal consultation. Written consent names the software, as ICMR's guidance on artificial intelligence expects consent and a human in control [D2-04-F35]. The approval and the message are the doctor's own act (chapter 4.4).
- **Measured:** days with valid readings per patient; proposals raised and how the doctor ruled, with reasons; time to rule; answers to the medicine question; any symptoms reported.
- **Must not be used to claim:** any change in pressure or control, safety, or clinical effect. Two weeks is shorter than one 30-day step, so few step-ups are expected.
- **Ethics:** a desk test on team members is not a clinical investigation on patients [D2-04-F50]. Whether this test counts as research needing an ethics committee is a question for the clinic and the university, not something this document decides.

OUR VIEW: rung 2 answers the first question that could stop the project: do doctors rule on proposals in time.

### 5.8 Rung 3: a 90-day pilot

OUR DESIGN unless cited.

**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days; patients who stop sending readings count as not controlled. It can move within three 30-day steps, control is what India's programme already reports, and counting silent patients tests the loop where the null Indian trial, mWellcare, did not look: between visits and among the patients who do not return (chapter 2.1).

**Secondary measures:** return or engagement rate (valid blocks a month); steps taken; time to approve; adverse events, including dizziness, falls and low readings.

| Comparison design | Can show | Cannot show |
|---|---|---|
| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |
| Matched clinics | A difference against similar clinics at the same time | Freedom from hidden differences between clinics |
| Staggered start (clinics switch on in random order, as in SMARThealth India [D2-01-F16]) | A fairer comparison, each clinic its own control | Quick results: it needs more clinics and time |

**Size** (OUR ARITHMETIC): to tell 40% from 55% controlled (ASSUMPTION) at 5% two-sided significance and 80% power needs 173 patients per arm; with 20% drop-out (ASSUMPTION), 217 per arm, 434 in all. This assumes patients are randomised one by one; randomising by clinic would need more, not computed here. The software build note's earlier sketch was about 300 patients over 6 months (OUR DESIGN).

**Approvals:** the steps in chapter 2.6 apply: a test licence, permission if the pilot counts as a clinical investigation, an ethics committee and trial registration before the first patient, and counsel's answer on whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides is a clinical investigation. Data duties under India's data protection rules start on 13 May 2027 by the gazette's wording (one law firm says a day earlier), inside a pilot that starts now [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20].

**Budget:** about ₹4.35-5.40 lakh for 217 loop-arm patients over 3 months (OUR ARITHMETIC), most of it cuffs at ₹1,849-2,334 each [D2-02-F30], with messages, health-worker calls and cloud costs as ASSUMPTION. Not included: doctor time, licence and ethics fees (not found in the notes), team costs.

**Three results that would make the team stop** (OUR VIEW):

1. Doctors leave most proposals unruled for days, so the loop stalls.
2. Most enrolled patients stop sending valid blocks within the first month; a US programme lost about 45% over its course [D2-01-F5].
3. Any serious harm linked to an approved step, such as symptomatic low pressure or a fall, that the safety branches did not catch.

### 5.9 The next 90 days

Five moves in order, from the strategy work; costs only where the notes hold a price.

| Move | Owner | Cost | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Freeze the engine; replay it on open home readings from 757 Ghanaian patients [D2-03-F61] | Engineering | A cuff, about ₹2,600 (search summary only) [D1-06-F31] | 36 of 36 branch tests pass; replay logged |
| 2. Sign a supervising physician and one clinic; set the low-pressure and lab limits left unset | Clinical | No price | A named doctor signs the protocol file |
| 3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to counsel; ask CDSCO (India's device regulator) for a class through its portal [D2-04-F11] | Business | Fees NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16] | Written answers on class, pilot permit and data duties |
| 4. Ten clinic conversations; test ₹99, ₹149 and ₹299 a month (ASSUMPTION); count cuff owners | Business | No price | Two signed letters, one naming a price |
| 5. File a 90-day pilot of about 300 patients with an ethics committee; register it before the first patient (search summary only) [D2-04-F45] | Clinical | Up to ₹7.8 lakh if every patient is lent a cuff (OUR ARITHMETIC: 300 x ₹2,600) | Submission accepted; registration filed |

OUR VIEW: moves 3 and 4 answer the two questions that chapter 3.2 marks as missing, whether anyone will pay and whether the loop can be defended.

Full detail: Appendix G (the protocol file, the decision steps, the test table, the hour-by-hour plan, the parts list, the hardware test, the simulation, the sample-size sum, the pilot budget, the draft Deep Tech Thesis and the hard questions).

OUR VIEW: tonight's win is a tested loop that a human approves, plus a simulation that honestly says the gain comes from contact. That is enough to build and show, but not enough to fund. Chapter 6 turns it into a recommendation, says what can and cannot be claimed at noon, and names the weak spots before anyone else does.

**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days; patients who stop sending readings count as not controlled. It can move within three 30-day steps, control is what India's programme already reports, and counting silent patients tests the loop where the null Indian trial, mWellcare, did not look: between visits and among the patients who do not return (chapter 2.1).

**Secondary measures:** return or engagement rate (valid blocks a month); steps taken; time to approve; adverse events, including dizziness, falls and low readings.

| Comparison design | Can show | Cannot show |
|---|---|---|
| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |
| Matched clinics | A difference against similar clinics at the same time | Freedom from hidden differences between clinics |
| Staggered start (clinics switch on in random order, as in SMARThealth India [D2-01-F16]) | A fairer comparison, each clinic its own control | Quick results: it needs more clinics and time |

**Size** (OUR ARITHMETIC): to tell 40% from 55% controlled (ASSUMPTION) at 5% two-sided significance and 80% power needs 173 patients per arm; with 20% drop-out (ASSUMPTION), 217 per arm, 434 in all. This assumes patients are randomised one by one; randomising by clinic would need more, not computed here. The software build note's earlier sketch was about 300 patients over 6 months (OUR DESIGN).

**Approvals:** the steps in chapter 2.6 apply: a test licence, permission if the pilot counts as a clinical investigation, an ethics committee and trial registration before the first patient, and counsel's answer on whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides is a clinical investigation. Data duties under India's data protection rules start on 13 May 2027 by the gazette's wording (one law firm says a day earlier), inside a pilot that starts now [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20].

**Budget:** about ₹4.35-5.40 lakh for 217 loop-arm patients over 3 months (OUR ARITHMETIC), most of it cuffs at ₹1,849-2,334 each [D2-02-F30], with messages, health-worker calls and cloud costs as ASSUMPTION. Not included: doctor time, licence and ethics fees (not found in the notes), team costs.

**Three results that would make the team stop** (OUR VIEW):

1. Doctors leave most proposals unruled for days, so the loop stalls.
2. Most enrolled patients stop sending valid blocks within the first month; a US programme lost about 45% over its course [D2-01-F5].
3. Any serious harm linked to an approved step, such as symptomatic low pressure or a fall, that the safety branches did not catch.

### 5.9 The next 90 days

Five moves in order, from the strategy work; costs only where the notes hold a price.

| Move | Owner | Cost | Done when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Freeze the engine; replay it on open home readings from 757 Ghanaian patients [D2-03-F61] | Engineering | A cuff, about ₹2,600 (search summary only) [D1-06-F31] | 36 of 36 branch tests pass; replay logged |
| 2. Sign a supervising physician and one clinic; set the low-pressure and lab limits left unset | Clinical | No price | A named doctor signs the protocol file |
| 3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to counsel; ask CDSCO (India's device regulator) for a class through its portal [D2-04-F11] | Business | Fees NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16] | Written answers on class, pilot permit and data duties |
| 4. Ten clinic conversations; test ₹99, ₹149 and ₹299 a month (ASSUMPTION); count cuff owners | Business | No price | Two signed letters, one naming a price |
| 5. File a 90-day pilot of about 300 patients with an ethics committee; register it before the first patient (search summary only) [D2-04-F45] | Clinical | Up to ₹7.8 lakh if every patient is lent a cuff (OUR ARITHMETIC: 300 x ₹2,600) | Submission accepted; registration filed |

OUR VIEW: moves 3 and 4 answer the two questions that chapter 3.2 marks as missing, whether anyone will pay and whether the loop can be defended.

Full detail: Appendix G (the protocol file, the decision steps, the test table, the hour-by-hour plan, the parts list, the hardware test, the simulation, the sample-size sum, the pilot budget, the draft Deep Tech Thesis and the hard questions).

OUR VIEW: tonight's win is a tested loop that a human approves, plus a simulation that honestly says the gain comes from contact. That is enough to build and show, but not enough to fund. Chapter 6 turns it into a recommendation, says what can and cannot be claimed at noon, and names the weak spots before anyone else does.

- **Software.** The `decide()` engine (chapter 4.2), in Python 3.11 with FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic and pytest. Three screens: the patient chat, the clinician queue, and a results page with the tests, coverage, the simulation chart, live-run counts, approve times and a dropdown to switch protocol.
- **Hardware.** The photo route and typed entry (chapter 4.3); Bluetooth through the omblepy tool only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand by about 02:00; the quality clip (chapter 4.5). A pill-box sensor is a stretch goal; a phone "taken" tap is the default. Cash outlay for one non-Bluetooth cuff and small parts is about ₹2,000-2,600 (OUR ARITHMETIC). Night delivery to Sonipat was not confirmed.
- **Protocol files.** The biology student owns them: Gujarat; Nigeria's losartan ladder as a second file, which covers adults 18 and over and has no lab check and no medicine-taken question [D1-06-F15]; and the American Diabetes Association's basal-insulin rule, on paper only, never run on a person. The claims check found four rules missing from the first Gujarat file (the age rule, the wider pregnancy rule, the abnormal-lab branch and the out-of-scope flag); they are now added.
- **Tests.** Thirty-six tests, one per listed branch, across both protocols and the insulin file. Four groups are still "to add", for the rules the claims check found: childbearing age, abnormal lab, outside the demo, and the Nigeria rules. Coverage target: every key in each file read by at least one test, plus line and branch coverage of `decide()`.
- **Team.** Six roles: E engine and I interfaces (computer science), P protocol and tests (biology), H1 clip and H2 cuff and photo route (hardware), L lead, story and simulation.
- **Checkpoints.** 02:00: a typed reading flows to a proposal, an approval and a message. 05:00: engine frozen. 09:30: testing stops; first dress rehearsal. 10:30: backup video recorded.
- **Cut lines.** If behind, drop in this order: WhatsApp; a third language; 20-seed simulation bands; the insulin file as tests (show the file only); Nigeria as a live dropdown (keep its tests); Telegram (use the web form); the photo or Bluetooth route (use typed readings). If the 02:00 checkpoint is missed, the first four go at once. Hardware falls back to one forearm sensor, no Bluetooth, and a phone tap for "taken".
- **Never cut:** the adherence check, the clinician approval step, the pregnancy and childbearing-age branch, the abnormal-lab branch, the "outside the demo" flag, the very-high branch, the test table and the safety statement.

The hardware is tested on 6 to 10 teammates, about 25 minutes each (OUR ESTIMATE). Volunteers agree verbally and are recorded by ID only; anyone at or above 180/110 is told to see a doctor and is not tested further. Each person is measured in correct posture, with the arm hanging at the side and with the arm on the lap, in coin-flip order, two readings each. The team reports counts and ranges, not p-values, and every failed photo and false alarm. This tests the pipeline and the clip, not cuff accuracy or patients.

OUR VIEW: the critical path is the schema, `decide()`, the first 29 tests, the queue with Approve, and the change message. Hardware hangs off it with a typed fallback, so a hardware failure costs a result, not the demo.

45	### 5.4 The four results the team can show honestly
46	
47	These are the only results that will exist by noon, with what each may and may not claim.
48	
49	| Result | What is measured | May claim | May not claim |
50	|---|---|---|---|
51	| (i) Branch coverage | Tests passing (target 36 of 36), line and branch coverage, protocol keys read | "The code does what the sheet says in every branch we listed" | "Safe", "clinically validated" |
52	| (ii) Simulated cohort | Control by month, needless step-ups, doctor workload | "Under stated assumptions, our model suggests..." | Any effect on patients |
53	| (iii) Live readings and clip | Readings received, share passing the gate, photo-to-stored time, photo accuracy, clip flags | "The pipeline works on real cuffs and real people" | Clinical data; that the clip improves control |
54	| (iv) Time to approve | Seconds per card and wrong taps, 3 people x 10 cards (OUR DESIGN) | "A person can rule on a card in about n seconds" | Clinical judgement; these are not clinicians on real patients |
55	
56	Teammates' readings will mostly give "same medicine"; the step path is shown with a labelled synthetic patient.
57	
58	**The simulated cohort** (OUR SIMULATION, not a trial, no effect on patients) follows 5,000 patients per arm for 12 monthly cycles. Each patient's hidden "responder step" (or none) is set from the government programme's Punjab control-by-step figures [D1-06-F04]; 48% are non-adherent (search summary only; definition-dependent) [D1-03-F44], used only to count needless step-ups. The clinic arm attends each month at the return rate of chapter 1, an ASSUMPTION that favours it; the loop arm sends a valid block in 30%, 50% or 70% of months (ASSUMPTION). In the first run (seed 1; to be re-run tonight, not quoted as data), control at month 12 was 39.0% in the clinic-only arm and 49.1%, 55.0% and 59.8% in the loop arm at those three levels (OUR SIMULATION).
59	
60	The build note's own reading: almost all the modelled gain comes from contact and refills, not smarter stepping, because the step curve is flat after step 3; the adherence check mainly cuts needless step-ups. Both follow from the assumptions. The clinic arm sits between district control and control among returners (chapter 1): plausible, not a validation. OUR VIEW: say this finding aloud; "the gain comes from contact" is more credible than a dosing claim.
61	
62	### 5.5 The 3-minute demo script
63	
64	OUR DESIGN, from the software build note:
65	
66	| Time | Who | On screen | Words |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| 0:00-0:25 | Lead | The programme's return and control figures (chapter 1) | "India's protocol works when patients come back. Half don't. We bring the 30-day visit home." |
69	| 0:25-0:50 | Lead | Loop diagram | "Reading in, protocol step out, doctor taps once, patient told in Hindi." |
70	| 0:50-1:30 | Patient teammate | Telegram: live cuff photo (or the clip); "2 good readings saved" | "Real reading, quality-checked." |
71	| 1:30-1:50 | Engine owner | Synthetic patient "Asha", 7 days near 148/92 on amlodipine 5 mg; adherence question, tap "0 days missed" | "Before stepping up, the protocol says check compliance. We ask." |
72	| 1:50-2:15 | Doctor (mentor or teammate) | Queue card with mean, readings, sheet line, guards; tap Approve; timer | "One tap. Every change is approved." |
73	| 2:15-2:30 | Patient teammate | Hindi message with the change and the doctor's name | "Change delivered in her language." |
74	| 2:30-2:50 | Biology student | Results page: 36 tests, coverage, simulation chart | "Every branch of the sheet tested. Our simulation, not a trial." |
75	| 2:50-3:00 | Lead | Switch the protocol to Nigeria; Asha's proposal becomes losartan 50 | "Same engine, any state's protocol." |
76	
77	Backup: the whole flow on the local web page, plus the 10:30 recording. Asha's synthetic record must say she is past childbearing age (OUR DESIGN); otherwise both sheets' pregnancy rules block the telmisartan and losartan steps.
78	
79	### 5.6 The safety statement
80	
81	Shown on the first slide and in the README, word for word from the software build note:
82	
83	> This is a student prototype built overnight. It is not medical advice and not a medical device. It does not diagnose or treat anyone. A clinician must approve every change of medicine; the software only drafts proposals from a published protocol. No patient data were used tonight. The readings shown are from teammates who volunteered and from synthetic patients; they are not clinical data. The simulation is our own model with stated assumptions, not a trial. Low-blood-pressure and lab-recency limits are deliberately left unset and must be set by a supervising clinician before any real use.
84	
85	Appendix G holds the draft one-page Deep Tech Thesis, corrected, with three blanks for tonight's numbers, and six hard questions with their answers.
86	
87	### 5.7 Rung 2: two weeks with a doctor in the loop
88	
89	OUR DESIGN. It asks whether the loop survives normal clinic work, not whether it lowers pressure.
90	
91	- **Setting:** one clinic; a few adults already on step 1 or 2; their own doctor rules on every proposal in a normal consultation. Written consent names the software, as ICMR's guidance on artificial intelligence expects consent and a human in control [D2-04-F35].
92	- **Measured:** days with valid readings per patient; proposals and how the doctor ruled, with reasons; time to rule; answers to the medicine question; any symptoms reported.
93	- **Must not be used to claim:** any change in pressure or control, safety, or clinical effect. Two weeks is shorter than one 30-day step, so few step-ups are expected.
94	- **Ethics:** a desk test on team members is not a clinical investigation on patients [D2-04-F50]. Whether this test counts as research needing an ethics committee is a question for the clinic and the university.
95	
96	OUR VIEW: rung 2 answers the first question that could stop the project: do doctors rule on proposals in time.
97	
98	### 5.8 Rung 3: a 90-day pilot
99	
100	OUR DESIGN unless cited.
101	
102	**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days, counting patients who stop sending readings as not controlled. It can move within three 30-day steps, it is the measure India's programme already reports, and counting silent patients tests the loop where the null Indian trial, mWellcare, did not look: between visits, among those who do not return (chapter 2.1).
103	
104	**Secondary measures:** valid blocks a month; steps taken; time to approve; adverse events, including dizziness, falls and low readings.
105	
106	| Comparison design | Can show | Cannot show |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |
109	| Matched clinics | A difference against similar clinics at the same time | Freedom from hidden differences |
110	| Staggered start (clinics switch on in random order, as in SMARThealth India [D2-01-F16]) | A fairer comparison, each clinic its own control | Quick results: it needs more clinics and time |
111	
112	**Size** (OUR ARITHMETIC): to tell 40% from 55% controlled (ASSUMPTION) at 5% two-sided significance and 80% power, with 20% drop-out (ASSUMPTION), needs 217 patients per arm, 434 in all, if patients are randomised one by one; randomising by clinic would need more, not computed here. The software build note's earlier sketch was about 300 patients over 6 months (OUR DESIGN).
113	
114	**Approvals:** the steps in chapter 2.6 apply: a test licence, permission if the pilot counts as a clinical investigation (a question for counsel), an ethics committee and trial registration before the first patient. Data duties under India's data protection rules start on 13 May 2027 by the gazette's wording (one law firm says a day earlier), inside a pilot that starts now [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20].
115	
116	**Budget:** about ₹4.35-5.40 lakh for 217 loop-arm patients over 3 months (OUR ARITHMETIC), mostly cuffs at ₹1,849-2,334 each [D2-02-F30]. Not included: doctor time, licence and ethics fees (not found in the notes), team costs.
117	
118	**Three results that would make the team stop** (OUR VIEW):
119	
120	1. Doctors leave most proposals unruled for days, so the loop stalls.
121	2. Most enrolled patients stop sending valid blocks within the first month; a US programme lost about 45% over its course [D2-01-F5].
122	3. Any serious harm linked to an approved step, such as symptomatic low pressure or a fall, that the safety branches did not catch.
123	
124	### 5.9 The next 90 days
125	
126	Five moves in order, from the strategy work; costs only where the notes hold a price.
127	
128	| Move | Owner | Cost | Done when |
129	|---|---|---|---|
130	| 1. Freeze the engine; replay it on open home readings from 757 Ghanaian patients [D2-03-F61] | Engineering | A cuff, about ₹2,600 (search summary only) [D1-06-F31] | 36 of 36 tests pass; replay logged |
131	| 2. Sign a supervising physician and one clinic; set the unset low-pressure and lab limits | Clinical | No price | A named doctor signs the protocol file |
132	| 3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to counsel; ask CDSCO (India's device regulator) for a class through its portal [D2-04-F11] | Business | Fees NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16] | Written answers on class, pilot permit and data duties |
133	| 4. Ten clinic conversations; test ₹99, ₹149 and ₹299 a month (ASSUMPTION); count cuff owners | Business | No price | Two signed letters, one naming a price |
134	| 5. File a 90-day pilot of about 300 patients with an ethics committee; register it before the first patient (search summary only) [D2-04-F45] | Clinical | Up to ₹7.8 lakh if every patient is lent a cuff (OUR ARITHMETIC: 300 x ₹2,600) | Submission accepted; registration filed |
135	
136	OUR VIEW: moves 3 and 4 answer the two rows that the question tree in chapter 3.2 marks as missing: will anyone pay, and can it be defended.
137	
138	Full detail: Appendix G (protocol file, test table, hour-by-hour plan, parts list, hardware test, simulation, sample-size sum, pilot budget, draft thesis, hard questions).
139	
140	OUR VIEW: tonight's win is a tested loop that a human approves, plus a simulation that honestly says the gain comes from contact. Do not trade that for a bigger claim. Chapter 6 turns it into a recommendation, says what can and cannot be claimed at noon, and names the weak spots before anyone else does.
141

input.content:
## 6. Recommendation, risks and open questions

This chapter brings the story to its answer. Chapters 1 to 3 showed the problem, what the research found and what it means; chapters 4 and 5 showed the product and tonight's build. What follows is what to do, how to say it at noon and to the mentor, where the idea is weak, and what the team still has to decide.

### 6.1 The recommendation

Build the home blood-pressure step loop tonight, and present it as the first protocol on a loop that can carry others. OUR VIEW, for three reasons.

1. **It is where the proof is strongest.** In the UK and US trials, pressure fell further than under usual care when a home reading led to a medicine change; in rural China, health workers stepping doses by protocol cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths, inside a programme that also gave cheaper medicines and paid for results; and an independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication (chapter 2.1).
2. **It is where India's gap is.** The government programme gets good control among patients who return, about half do not return, and only about one in five people with high blood pressure is controlled in its first nine districts (chapter 1). No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the protocol model of the government's open-source app (chapter 2.4).
3. **It can be built and tested honestly by noon.** The state protocol is public, down to the doses and the 30-day interval (chapter 4.1), and the programme's own control-by-step figures give a base for a simulated cohort (chapter 5.4).

Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion (chapter 4.8). Who does what:

- **Software:** the protocol engine, the patient chat, the doctor's approval screen, the test harness.
- **Hardware:** read the cuff (a phone photo of any cuff's screen, with the person confirming the digits; typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand), and build the clip that checks arm position and stillness, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change.
- **Biology:** encode the protocol and its safety branches, write the test cases, own the clinical story.

### 6.2 The pitch in one breath

OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."

### 6.3 What you can say at noon, and what you cannot

| You can say | You cannot say |
|---|---|
| Every branch of two published protocols passes our tests. | The product is safe, validated or approved. |
| A simulation of ours, built on the programme's own figures, shows where the gain would come from. | The loop improves control. No patient has used it. |
| Readings from teammates flowed end to end, and this share passed the quality check. | These are clinical data. |
| A doctor approves every change; the software only drafts. | The software prescribes or treats. |
| It is a student prototype, not a medical device. | It complies with any rule. India's new guidance treats such software as a device (chapter 2.6). |

### 6.4 What we are not claiming

- **No benefit to patients has been shown.** Tonight's results are code tests, a simulation of our own, and readings from teammates.
- **It is not a medical device and not cleared by anyone.** India's guidance treats software of this kind as a regulated device, with the class depending on how the condition is graded, and with no exemption for tools that only a clinician sees (chapter 2.6).
- **The scores, the market model and the price are ours.** No customer has been interviewed.

### 6.5 The three weak spots

Own these before someone else raises them.

1. **Who pays.** Public-sector treatment "could be as low as Rs 200 per patient per year" (WHO India, 2022) [D2-01-F12], so a state will not pay app-scale prices. Outpatient insurance cover is tiny (search summary only) [D2-05-F10]. Our price of ₹149 a patient a month is an ASSUMPTION, and at that price the US$100 million-a-year test fails in India alone (OUR ARITHMETIC, chapter 2.5). The companies that died abroad sold software without a payer (chapter 1).
2. **It will be regulated**, and a study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first [D2-04-F13, D2-04-F14]. The honest path is clinician-approved proposals at one partner clinic under ethics approval, then a licence.
3. **An Indian trial of clinic decision support found nothing.** In mWellcare, prompting nurses and doctors during visits added no significant gain over well-run usual care (chapter 2.1). The loop has to earn its value between visits and among the patients who do not return. If a pilot shows no gain in return rate or control, that is the result that stops the project.

### 6.6 Why not the other options

OUR VIEW, from the scores and reasons in chapter 3.3.

| Option | Why it is not the first build |
|---|---|
| Insulin dose guidance | Good trials, but no open type 2 simulator for an honest test tonight [D1-06-F30], a real risk of low blood sugar, and a dosing app from a large medicine maker already exists. Shown tonight as the second protocol, on paper. |
| Adaptive home rehabilitation | Easy to demo, but software rehabilitation matches in-person care without beating usual care, and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C licence for cardiac rehabilitation. |
| Heart-failure dose loop | Strong outcome proof and the largest unmet need far from a specialist [D1-01-F31, D1-01-F35], but it needs lab values, so it cannot be tested honestly tonight. The later protocol. |
| Breathing plan with a sensor | The dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor [D1-02-F37], and sensor inhalers failed commercially. |
| Warfarin self-dosing | The best proof of all, a small market, and no meter tonight. |
| Weight-loss injection companion | A hot market after generic semaglutide, no outcome evidence yet [D1-01-F41], and three Indian players already in. |
| A drug-free arm: handgrip exercise dosed by a load-cell device | Checked late in the night and set aside: the one sham-controlled trial found no significant change [D3-08-F10], and the main device received a US regulator's warning letter in 2019 [D3-08-F27]. A possible later arm once the evidence firms up (Appendix F). |

### 6.7 Pitching to the mentor

The mentor's fund (chapter 1) led a 2023 round in Wellthy, an Indian digital-therapeutics company [D3-06-F01]. By its chief executive's account, its first investment, in 2015, was CureApp, the Japanese company whose blood-pressure app is covered by insurance there (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F26]. That app coaches lifestyle and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. The home step loop is the piece neither had: the reading changes the medicine. Say that plainly, and be ready for the question the Wellthy story raises, which is who pays.

OUR VIEW: he modelled outcome-based contracts for his master's thesis, so expect him to ask what outcome changes, by how much, and who checks it. He has promoted an open-mic format of an 8-minute pitch with no slides (Appendix H), so practise telling the whole loop that way: patient, reading, dose step, clinician approval, outcome.

**How to frame it** (OUR VIEW):

1. **One outcome, measured one way:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned, set against the fall a US review counts as meaningful (chapter 2.1). Show how each home reading is checked for posture and repeats.
2. **The easiest wedge.** His partner asks for the "easiest" wedge into a large market [D2-07-F14]. Blood pressure is it: the largest patient pool (chapter 1), a cheap cuff (chapter 5.9) and a step protocol already in government text (chapter 4.1). The same engine loads an insulin protocol next.
3. **Prototype to product.** Tonight: every protocol branch tested, a clinician approving each change. Next: a 90-day pilot. The partner says investors like to enter between an alpha prototype and a beta customer pilot.
4. **A real Japan angle.** Name only Panasonic's health and wellness theme [D2-07-F9], the CII healthcare delegation and the Intralink event (Appendix H). Claim no Japanese partner.
5. **Say the null result first.** mWellcare found no difference (chapter 2.1); our loop works between visits, where that trial did not look.

**Five questions to expect:**

| Question | Honest answer |
|---|---|
| What outcome changes, by how much? | Point to HyperLink, the US trial of pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings (chapter 2.1). We have no patient data of our own. |
| Is this just a rules engine? | The rules are what the trials show works, and nobody runs them at home. The hard parts are trusting a home reading, telling a missed dose from a needed step-up, and proving safety; adherence tools alone failed (chapter 2.1). |
| Who pays? | Not known yet. Firms selling an app alone died (chapter 1). |
| Is it safe and legal? | A clinician approves every change; unsafe cases go up. The regulatory class is still open. |
| Will patients stay? | A clinician's referral keeps people in remote programmes longer (chapter 2.1). Only 63.6% of women aged 15-49 owned a phone in 2023-24 (search summary only) [D1-03-F42], so it must work on a shared one. |

**Five questions worth asking him:**

1. Your fund led Wellthy's 2023 round and Wellthy now sits inside TruDoc: who ended up paying for that kind of chronic-disease programme, and what would you do differently?
2. What evidence would you want before a pilot: 90-day control, or something harder?
3. Does anyone in the Panasonic programme or the CII corridor work on home measurement?
4. How does the campus pre-incubation route work, and can an Ashoka team enter it?
5. Could Biomoneta or Anaut share how they handled device approval?

### 6.8 Open decisions for the team

| Decision | Options | What would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| First customer | A private clinic chain; a district programme; a non-profit that runs hypertension care | Three conversations next week (discussion guide in Appendix F) |
| Who approves a step | A doctor only; later a health officer under a written order | A lawyer's answer. No order letting a health officer change a dose was found [D3-05-F30], and the telemedicine guidelines want the registered doctor to deliver the prescription directly (chapter 2.6) |
| How the reading comes in | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the person (tonight's route); typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand | Tonight's test of the photo reader on teammates |
| The home line | 135/85 at home for a protocol written for 140/90 in clinic (OUR DESIGN, chapter 4.3) | A clinician's signature on the protocol file |
| Open or closed | Give the engine to the public programme's open-source app; keep it proprietary | Who the first customer is |
| Second protocol | Insulin; heart failure | Whether a diagnostics partner for lab values can be found |

### 6.9 The next seven days

1. Interview one general doctor, two patients on blood-pressure medicine with a family member, one pharmacist and one health worker, using the guide in Appendix F.
2. Ask one clinic whether its doctor would approve proposals for ten of their own patients for two weeks (rung 2, chapter 5.7), and what paperwork they would need.
3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to a lawyer or a regulatory consultant.
4. Rerun the simulation with engagement figures from the two-week test in place of assumptions.
5. Write up tonight's four results with their limits, and send them to the mentor with one clear ask.

### 6.10 What this document does not cover

Chapter 7 and the claim register in Appendix J list what was not found and what was not re-checked. The largest gaps are customer interviews, a measured split of public and private treatment, current specialist counts, and any Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps.

Full detail: Appendix F (the options, the frameworks and the handgrip arm), Appendix H (the mentor and the fund) and Appendix E (the rules and the three questions for a lawyer).

OUR VIEW: the medicine is settled; payment and defence are not. ## 6. Recommendation, risks and open questions

This chapter brings the story to its answer. Chapters 1 to 3 showed the problem, what the research found and what it means; chapters 4 and 5 showed the product and tonight's build. What follows is what to do, how to say it at noon and to the mentor, where the idea is weak, and what the team still has to decide.

### 6.1 The recommendation

Build the home blood-pressure step loop tonight, and present it as the first protocol on a loop that can carry others. OUR VIEW, for three reasons.

1. **It is where the proof is strongest.** In the UK and US trials, pressure fell further than under usual care when a home reading led to a medicine change; in rural China, health workers stepping doses by protocol cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths, inside a programme that also gave cheaper medicines and paid for results; and an independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication (chapter 2.1).
2. **It is where India's gap is.** The government programme gets good control among patients who return, about half do not return, and only about one in five people with high blood pressure is controlled in its first nine districts (chapter 1). No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the protocol model of the government's open-source app (chapter 2.4).
3. **It can be built and tested honestly by noon.** The state protocol is public, down to the doses and the 30-day interval (chapter 4.1), and the programme's own control-by-step figures give a base for a simulated cohort (chapter 5.4).

Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion (chapter 4.8). Who does what:

- **Software:** the protocol engine, the patient chat, the doctor's approval screen, the test harness.
- **Hardware:** read the cuff (a phone photo of any cuff's screen, with the person confirming the digits; typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand), and build the clip that checks arm position and stillness, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change.
- **Biology:** encode the protocol and its safety branches, write the test cases, own the clinical story.

### 6.2 The pitch in one breath

OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."

### 6.3 What you can say at noon, and what you cannot

| You can say | You cannot say |
|---|---|
| Every branch of two published protocols passes our tests. | The product is safe, validated or approved. |
| A simulation of ours, built on the programme's own figures, shows where the gain would come from. | The loop improves control. No patient has used it. |
| Readings from teammates flowed end to end, and this share passed the quality check. | These are clinical data. |
| A doctor approves every change; the software only drafts. | The software prescribes or treats. |
| It is a student prototype, not a medical device. | It complies with any rule. India's new guidance treats such software as a device (chapter 2.6). |

### 6.4 What we are not claiming

- **No benefit to patients has been shown.** Tonight's results are code tests, a simulation of our own, and readings from teammates.
- **It is not a medical device and not cleared by anyone.** India's guidance treats software of this kind as a regulated device, with the class depending on how the condition is graded, and with no exemption for tools that only a clinician sees (chapter 2.6).
- **The scores, the market model and the price are ours.** No customer has been interviewed.

### 6.5 The three weak spots

Own these before someone else raises them.

1. **Who pays.** Public-sector treatment "could be as low as Rs 200 per patient per year" (WHO India, 2022) [D2-01-F12], so a state will not pay app-scale prices. Outpatient insurance cover is tiny (search summary only) [D2-05-F10]. Our price of ₹149 a patient a month is an ASSUMPTION, and at that price the US$100 million-a-year test fails in India alone (OUR ARITHMETIC, chapter 2.5). The companies that died abroad sold software without a payer (chapter 1).
2. **It will be regulated**, and a study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first [D2-04-F13, D2-04-F14]. The honest path is clinician-approved proposals at one partner clinic under ethics approval, then a licence.
3. **An Indian trial of clinic decision support found nothing.** In mWellcare, prompting nurses and doctors during visits added no significant gain over well-run usual care (chapter 2.1). The loop has to earn its value between visits and among the patients who do not return. If a pilot shows no gain in return rate or control, that is the result that stops the project.

### 6.6 Why not the other options

OUR VIEW, from the scores and reasons in chapter 3.3.

| Option | Why it is not the first build |
|---|---|
| Insulin dose guidance | Good trials, but no open type 2 simulator for an honest test tonight [D1-06-F30], a real risk of low blood sugar, and a dosing app from a large medicine maker already exists. Shown tonight as the second protocol, on paper. |
| Adaptive home rehabilitation | Easy to demo, but software rehabilitation matches in-person care without beating usual care, and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C licence for cardiac rehabilitation. |
| Heart-failure dose loop | Strong outcome proof and the largest unmet need far from a specialist [D1-01-F31, D1-01-F35], but it needs lab values, so it cannot be tested honestly tonight. The later protocol. |
| Breathing plan with a sensor | The dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor [D1-02-F37], and sensor inhalers failed commercially. |
| Warfarin self-dosing | The best proof of all, a small market, and no meter tonight. |
| Weight-loss injection companion | A hot market after generic semaglutide, no outcome evidence yet [D1-01-F41], and three Indian players already in. |
| A drug-free arm: handgrip exercise dosed by a load-cell device | Checked late in the night and set aside: the one sham-controlled trial found no significant change [D3-08-F10], and the main device received a US regulator's warning letter in 2019 [D3-08-F27]. A possible later arm once the evidence firms up (Appendix F). |

### 6.7 Pitching to the mentor

The mentor's fund (chapter 1) led a 2023 round in Wellthy, an Indian digital-therapeutics company [D3-06-F01]. By its chief executive's account, its first investment, in 2015, was CureApp, the Japanese company whose blood-pressure app is covered by insurance there (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F26]. That app coaches lifestyle and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. The home step loop is the piece neither had: the reading changes the medicine. Say that plainly, and be ready for the question the Wellthy story raises, which is who pays.

OUR VIEW: he modelled outcome-based contracts for his master's thesis, so expect him to ask what outcome changes, by how much, and who checks it. He has promoted an open-mic format of an 8-minute pitch with no slides (Appendix H), so practise telling the whole loop that way: patient, reading, dose step, clinician approval, outcome.

**How to frame it** (OUR VIEW):

1. **One outcome, measured one way:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned, set against the fall a US review counts as meaningful (chapter 2.1). Show how each home reading is checked for posture and repeats.
2. **The easiest wedge.** His partner asks for the "easiest" wedge into a large market [D2-07-F14]. Blood pressure is it: the largest patient pool (chapter 1), a cheap cuff (chapter 5.9) and a step protocol already in government text (chapter 4.1). The same engine loads an insulin protocol next.
3. **Prototype to product.** Tonight: every protocol branch tested, a clinician approving each change. Next: a 90-day pilot. The partner says investors like to enter between an alpha prototype and a beta customer pilot.
4. **A real Japan angle.** Name only Panasonic's health and wellness theme [D2-07-F9], the CII healthcare delegation and the Intralink event (Appendix H). Claim no Japanese partner.
5. **Say the null result first.** mWellcare found no difference (chapter 2.1); our loop works between visits, where that trial did not look.

**Five questions to expect:**

| Question | Honest answer |
|---|---|
| What outcome changes, by how much? | Point to HyperLink, the US trial of pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings (chapter 2.1). We have no patient data of our own. |
| Is this just a rules engine? | The rules are what the trials show works, and nobody runs them at home. The hard parts are trusting a home reading, telling a missed dose from a needed step-up, and proving safety; adherence tools alone failed (chapter 2.1). |
| Who pays? | Not known yet. Firms selling an app alone died (chapter 1). |
| Is it safe and legal? | A clinician approves every change; unsafe cases go up. The regulatory class is still open. |
| Will patients stay? | A clinician's referral keeps people in remote programmes longer (chapter 2.1). Only 63.6% of women aged 15-49 owned a phone in 2023-24 (search summary only) [D1-03-F42], so it must work on a shared one. |

**Five questions worth asking him:**

1. Your fund led Wellthy's 2023 round and Wellthy now sits inside TruDoc: who ended up paying for that kind of chronic-disease programme, and what would you do differently?
2. What evidence would you want before a pilot: 90-day control, or something harder?
3. Does anyone in the Panasonic programme or the CII corridor work on home measurement?
4. How does the campus pre-incubation route work, and can an Ashoka team enter it?
5. Could Biomoneta or Anaut share how they handled device approval?

### 6.8 Open decisions for the team

| Decision | Options | What would settle it |
|---|---|---|
| First customer | A private clinic chain; a district programme; a non-profit that runs hypertension care | Three conversations next week (discussion guide in Appendix F) |
| Who approves a step | A doctor only; later a health officer under a written order | A lawyer's answer. No order letting a health officer change a dose was found [D3-05-F30], and the telemedicine guidelines want the registered doctor to deliver the prescription directly (chapter 2.6) |
| How the reading comes in | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the person (tonight's route); typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand | Tonight's test of the photo reader on teammates |
| The home line | 135/85 at home for a protocol written for 140/90 in clinic (OUR DESIGN, chapter 4.3) | A clinician's signature on the protocol file |
| Open or closed | Give the engine to the public programme's open-source app; keep it proprietary | Who the first customer is |
| Second protocol | Insulin; heart failure | Whether a diagnostics partner for lab values can be found |

### 6.9 The next seven days

1. Interview one general doctor, two patients on blood-pressure medicine with a family member, one pharmacist and one health worker, using the guide in Appendix F.
2. Ask one clinic whether its doctor would approve proposals for ten of their own patients for two weeks (rung 2, chapter 5.7), and what paperwork they would need.
3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to a lawyer or a regulatory consultant.
4. Rerun the simulation with engagement figures from the two-week test in place of assumptions.
5. Write up tonight's four results with their limits, and send them to the mentor with one clear ask.

### 6.10 What this document does not cover

Chapter 7 and the claim register in Appendix J list what was not found and what was not re-checked. The largest gaps are customer interviews, a measured split of public and private treatment, current specialist counts, and any Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps.

Full detail: Appendix F (the options, the frameworks and the handgrip arm), Appendix H (the mentor and the fund) and Appendix E (the rules and the three questions for a lawyer).

OUR VIEW: the medicine is settled; payment and defence are not. A prototype alone is not fundable, and the next proof is a signed pilot clinic, a doctor who signs the protocol and a class answer from the regulator. Chapter 7 explains how this document was made and how far to trust each number in it.

### 1.5 The market issues: why the market has not fixed this

The gap is clear, so the next thing to explain is why companies have not filled it. Three answers recur in the notes: what has been sold stops before the dose, the companies that sold apps on their own ran out of money, and nobody yet pays for the step that is missing.

#### What has been sold so far

India's private chronic-care programmes sell a glucose sensor or meter plus a doctor and a coach. None of their pages says glucose data changes a drug dose by algorithm, so on what is published they sit at adaptive depth 3 [D1-04-F02, D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. Their outcome figures are their own averages with no comparison group (THEIR CLAIM) [D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07]. The patient pays: Sugar.fit charges ₹29,990 for 12 months or ₹15,990 for 4 months (13 Nov 2026) [D1-04-F04], and HealthifyRx charged ₹48,000 for 3 months (May 2025) [D1-04-F26].

The government's tools stop at the same place. IHCI runs a fixed state drug-and-dose protocol, and its Simple app keeps a registry, flags overdue patients and sends reminders [D1-04-F19]. The app's protocol model stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it [D1-06-F40]. So the nurse records the reading, but the step-up decision still waits for a visit.

#### Why companies died

Abroad, several companies sold digital therapeutics (software that changes one patient's treatment) or sensors, some with good trials, and failed. India's best-funded chronic-care app did too.

| Company | What it sold | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Pear Therapeutics (US) | Prescription apps for addiction and insomnia, with randomised trials [D1-02-F17] | Bankrupt April 2023; assets sold for just over $6M against $130M of liabilities [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F42]. A panel said it tried to change care and payment at once [D1-05-F21] |
| Akili (US) | A game for ADHD in children | $523,000 of prescription revenue in 2023, net loss $59.5M; sale agreed for about $34M in May 2024 [D1-02-F44] |
| Better Therapeutics (US) | A diabetes app: HbA1c 0.39 points lower than a control app (669 patients, 90 days) [D1-02-F21] | Expected no revenue in 2023 (revenue not reported), deficit $134.3M; weighed winding down in March 2024 [D1-02-F46] |
| Teva Digihaler | Sensor inhalers and app | US distribution and app support stopped 1 June 2024; the US notice gave no reason and a UK recall cited "commercial reasons" [D1-02-F41] |
| PhableCare (India) | Blood-pressure and glucose devices, consultations (depth 2) | Raised ₹187 crore in Apr 2022; stopped work in Feb 2023; staff fell from about 2,000 to 200, many unpaid. Former staff said there were no funds; the founders blamed staff misconduct [D1-04-F14, D1-04-F23] |

The common causes, as the notes give them:

- No one paid for the app alone [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F44, D1-05-F23].
- Too few prescribers, and trials that payers did not accept as outcome proof [D1-05-F21].
- Sensors with no therapy change [D1-02-F41, D1-02-F02].
- Valuations ahead of revenue, then no cash [D1-05-F55, D1-04-F23].
- Users leave fast: across 93 mental-health apps, the median app kept 3.3% of its users at day 30 [D1-02-F26].

#### Who pays today

In India, the patient pays for private programmes, as above, and the state pays for public care, where treatment "could be as low as Rs 200 per patient per year", a modelled drug cost that leaves out staff (WHO, 2022; SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D2-01-F12, D2-05-F18, D3-05-F09]. The notes found no Indian payer, public or private, that pays for remote blood-pressure monitoring or a digital therapeutic as a line item [D2-04-F47]. Insurance barely touches outpatient care: outpatient cover is below 0.1% of a US$37.7 billion outpatient market (industry-sponsored, search summary only) [D2-05-F10].

Abroad, the firms that reached scale are paid by someone other than the patient. Employers and insurers pay for clinician-led programmes: Hinge Health, paid "primarily" by employers, had revenue of $234.97M in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16]. Or the company sells a device that delivers the therapy: Insulet, a closed-loop insulin pump maker, had revenue of $842.0M in the same quarter [D1-05-F41].

#### No dose change found

No Indian service was found that turns home blood-pressure or glucose readings into a medicine change between visits [D1-04-F09, D1-04-F19]. This was one agent's limited search on 13 Nov 2026, a search result and not proof of absence; chapter 2.4 lists the searches and the nearest products abroad.

OUR VIEW: India's best-funded chronic-care app ran out of money within a year of its largest round. Money raised is not proof that anyone will pay. The doctor controls the prescription and the payer controls the money; a product that leaves either out has no user or no buyer.

### 1.6 The problem in one paragraph

OUR VIEW. Hundreds of millions of Indians have high blood pressure or diabetes, many are on medicine, and few are controlled. India already screens and enrols them at crore scale, and its programme has a protocol and free drugs. What it lacks between visits is the decision, the confirmation and the action. The scarce thing is the prescriber's decision, which waits for a visit that about half the patients do not make, and when they do come, the visit lasts about two minutes. The products sold so far show readings, send reminders or coach, and stop before the dose; companies that sold an app on its own, even with good trials, failed for lack of a payer.

Full detail: Appendix A (the challenge, the burden and the voices), with Appendix D for the companies and Appendix E for who pays.

The problem is now clear: a large, treatable population, a system that loses half of it between visits, and a market that watches and reminds but does not change the treatment. The next chapter asks what the research says actually works, and whether anyone has made it work without specialists.
