3	This chapter brings the story to its answer. After the problem, the research, the analysis, the product and the build, it says what to do, how to say it, where the idea is weak, and what the team still has to decide.
4	
5	### 6.1 The recommendation
6	
7	Build the home blood-pressure step loop tonight, and present it as the first protocol on a loop that can carry others. OUR VIEW, for three reasons.
8	
9	1. **It is where the proof is strongest.** In the UK and US trials, pressure fell further than under usual care when a home reading led to a medicine change; in rural China, health workers stepping doses by protocol cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths, inside a programme that also gave cheaper medicines and paid for results; and an independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication (chapter 2.1).
10	2. **It is where India's gap is.** The government programme gets good control among patients who return, about half do not return, and only about one in five people with high blood pressure is controlled in its first nine districts (chapter 1). No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the government app's protocol model (chapter 1.5).
11	3. **It can be built and tested honestly by noon.** The state protocol is public, down to the doses and the 30-day interval (chapter 4.1), and the programme's own control-by-step figures give a base for a simulated cohort (chapter 5.4).
12	
13	Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion (chapter 4.8). Software builds the engine, the patient chat, the approval screen and the test harness. Hardware reads the cuff (photo confirmed by the person, typed entry as fallback, Bluetooth only with a suitable cuff) and builds the clip, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change. Biology encodes the protocol and its safety branches, writes the test cases and owns the clinical story.
14	
15	### 6.2 The pitch in one breath
16	
17	OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."
18	
19	### 6.3 What you can say at noon, and what you cannot
20	
21	| You can say | You cannot say |
22	|---|---|
23	| Every branch of two published protocols passes our tests. | The product is safe, validated or approved. |
24	| A simulation of ours, built on the programme's own figures, shows where the gain would come from. | The loop improves control. No patient has used it. |
25	| Readings from teammates flowed end to end, and this share passed the quality check. | These are clinical data. |
26	| A doctor approves every change; the software only drafts. | The software prescribes or treats. |
27	| It is a student prototype, not a medical device. | It complies with any rule. India's new guidance treats such software as a device (chapter 2.6). |
28	
29	What we are not claiming: any benefit to patients, since tonight's results are code tests, our own simulation and teammates' readings; that the loop is a cleared device, when India's guidance gives no exemption for tools only a clinician sees (chapter 2.6); or that the scores, the market model and the price are more than ours, with no customer interviewed.
30	
31	### 6.4 The three weak spots
32	
33	Own these before someone else raises them.
34	
35	1. **Who pays.** Public treatment is cheap enough that a state will not pay app-scale prices, and outpatient insurance cover is tiny (chapter 1.5). Our price of ₹149 a patient a month is an ASSUMPTION, and at that price the US$100 million-a-year test fails in India alone (OUR ARITHMETIC, chapter 2.5). The companies that died abroad sold software without a payer (chapter 1.5).
36	2. **It will be regulated**, and a study on patients needs permission and ethics approval first [D2-04-F13, D2-04-F14]. The honest path is clinician-approved proposals at one partner clinic under ethics approval, then a licence.
37	3. **An Indian trial of clinic decision support found nothing.** In mWellcare, prompting nurses and doctors during visits added no significant gain over well-run usual care (chapter 2.1). The loop has to earn its value between visits, among the patients who do not return. If a pilot shows no gain in return rate or control, that result stops the project.
38	
39	### 6.5 Why not the other options
40	
41	OUR VIEW, from the scores and reasons in chapter 3.3.
42	
43	| Option | Why it is not the first build |
44	|---|---|
45	| Insulin dose guidance | Good trials, but no open type 2 simulator for an honest test tonight [D1-06-F30], a real risk of low blood sugar, and a large medicine maker's dosing app already exists. Shown as the second protocol, on paper. |
46	| Adaptive home rehabilitation | Easy to demo, but it matches in-person care without beating usual care, and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C licence for cardiac rehabilitation. |
47	| Heart-failure dose loop | Strong outcome proof and the largest unmet need far from a specialist [D1-01-F31, D1-01-F35], but it needs lab values, so no honest test tonight. The later protocol. |
48	| Breathing plan with a sensor | The dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor [D1-02-F37], and sensor inhalers failed commercially. |
49	| Warfarin self-dosing | The best proof of all, a small market, and no meter tonight. |
50	| Weight-loss injection companion | A hot market after generic semaglutide, no outcome evidence yet [D1-01-F41], and three Indian players already in. |
51	| Handgrip exercise dosed by a load-cell device | A drug-free arm, set aside late in the night: the one sham-controlled trial found no significant change [D3-08-F10], and the main device drew a US regulator's warning letter in 2019 [D3-08-F27]. A possible later arm (Appendix F). |
52	
53	### 6.6 Pitching to the mentor
54	
55	The mentor's fund (chapter 1.1) led a 2023 round in Wellthy, an Indian digital-therapeutics company [D3-06-F01]. By its chief executive's account, its first investment, in 2015, was CureApp, the Japanese company whose blood-pressure app is covered by insurance there (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F26]. That app coaches lifestyle and does not change medicines [D3-06-F19]. The home step loop is the piece neither had: the reading changes the medicine. Say that plainly, and be ready for the question the Wellthy story raises: who pays.
56	
57	OUR VIEW: he modelled outcome-based contracts for his master's thesis, so expect him to ask what outcome changes, by how much, and who checks it. He has promoted an 8-minute, no-slides pitch format (Appendix H): practise the whole loop that way, from patient to outcome.
58	
59	**How to frame it** (OUR VIEW):
60	
61	1. **One outcome, measured one way:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned, set against the fall a US review counts as meaningful (chapter 2.1), with each reading checked for posture and repeats.
62	2. **The easiest wedge.** His partner asks for the "easiest" wedge into a large market [D2-07-F14]. Blood pressure is it: the largest patient pool (chapter 1), a cheap cuff and a step protocol already in government text (chapter 4.1). The same engine loads insulin next.
63	3. **Prototype to product.** Tonight a tested loop; next a 90-day pilot. The partner says investors like to enter between an alpha prototype and a beta customer pilot.
64	4. **A real Japan angle.** Name only Panasonic's health and wellness theme [D2-07-F9], the CII healthcare delegation and the Intralink event (Appendix H). Claim no Japanese partner.
65	5. **Say the null result first:** mWellcare (chapter 2.1). Our loop works between visits, where that trial did not look.
66	
67	| Question to expect | Honest answer |
68	|---|---|
69	| What outcome changes, by how much? | Point to HyperLink, the US trial of pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings (chapter 2.1). We have no patient data of our own. |
70	| Is this just a rules engine? | The rules are what the trials show works, and nobody runs them at home. The hard parts are trusting a home reading, telling a missed dose from a needed step-up, and proving safety; adherence tools alone failed (chapter 2.1). |
71	| Who pays? | Not known yet. Firms selling an app alone died (chapter 1.5). |
72	| Is it safe and legal? | A clinician approves every change; unsafe cases go up. The regulatory class is still open. |
73	| Will patients stay? | A clinician's referral keeps people in remote programmes longer (chapter 2.1); many women have no phone of their own (chapter 1.3), so it must work on a shared one. |
74	
75	**Five questions worth asking him:**
76	
77	1. Your fund led Wellthy's 2023 round and Wellthy now sits inside TruDoc: who ended up paying for that kind of chronic-disease programme, and what would you do differently?
78	2. What evidence would you want before a pilot: 90-day control, or something harder?
79	3. Does anyone in the Panasonic programme or the CII corridor work on home measurement?
80	4. How does the campus pre-incubation route work, and can an Ashoka team enter it?
81	5. Could Biomoneta or Anaut share how they handled device approval?
82	
83	### 6.7 Open decisions for the team
84	
85	| Decision | Options | What would settle it |
86	|---|---|---|
87	| First customer | A private clinic chain; a district programme; a non-profit that runs hypertension care | Three conversations next week (discussion guide in Appendix F) |
88	| Who approves a step | A doctor only; later a health officer under a written order | A lawyer's answer. No order letting a health officer change a dose was found [D3-05-F30], and the telemedicine guidelines want the registered doctor to deliver the prescription directly (chapter 2.6) |
89	| How the reading comes in | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the person (tonight); typed entry; Bluetooth only with a suitable cuff | Tonight's test of the photo reader on teammates |
90	| The home line | 135/85 at home for a protocol written for 140/90 in clinic (OUR DESIGN, chapter 4.3) | A clinician's signature on the protocol file |
91	| Open or closed | Give the engine to the public programme's open-source app; keep it proprietary | Who the first customer is |
92	| Second protocol | Insulin; heart failure | Whether a diagnostics partner for lab values can be found |
93	
94	### 6.8 The next seven days
95	
96	1. Interview one general doctor, two patients on blood-pressure medicine with a family member, one pharmacist and one health worker, using the guide in Appendix F.
97	2. Ask one clinic whether its doctor would approve proposals for ten of their own patients for two weeks (rung 2, chapter 5.7), and what paperwork they would need.
98	3. Put the three questions for a lawyer (Appendix E) to a lawyer or a regulatory consultant.
99	4. Rerun the simulation with engagement figures from the two-week test in place of assumptions.
100	5. Write up tonight's four results with their limits, and send them to the mentor with one clear ask.
101	
102	### 6.9 What this document does not cover
103	
104	Chapter 7 and the claim register in Appendix J list what was not found and not re-checked. The largest gaps: customer interviews, a measured public-private split of treatment, current specialist counts, and any Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps.
105	
106	Full detail: Appendix F (the options, the frameworks, the handgrip arm), Appendix H (the mentor and the fund) and Appendix E (the rules and the questions for a lawyer).
107	
108	OUR VIEW: the medicine is settled; payment and defence are not. A prototype alone is not fundable; the next proof is a signed pilot clinic, a doctor who signs the protocol, and a class answer from the regulator. Chapter 7 explains how this document was made and how far to trust it.
109

For patients who keep coming, the protocol works. In Punjab and Maharashtra, 70% and 76% of patients seen again were controlled on amlodipine 5 mg alone, and 75% and 81% after step 2 [D3-05-F04]. Across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82%; about 43% of starters are missing from that count [D1-06-F04]. The drugs are cheap: using amlodipine for the first two steps cut drug cost about 20%, from US$2.50 to US$2.05 per patient per year. Neither figure includes staff, and a full cost was not found [D3-05-F05].
--- 167
- **Insulin titration rules.** The American Diabetes Association's 2025 rule starts basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, steps it every 3 days towards a fasting target, and lowers it by 10-20% after a low with no clear reason [D1-06-F16]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17].

- **Blood-pressure ladders.** Fixed steps with a 30-day review, lab and pregnancy guards, and referral at the end (chapter 4.1) [D1-06-F14]. People do differ: PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if the drug were chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].

1	## 4. The product we can build
2	
3	Chapter 3 ended with a choice: the home blood-pressure step loop. This chapter shows that product end to end: what it does, what the patient and the doctor see, and the checks that stop a bad reading or a missed tablet from changing a dose. It ends with how the same loop can carry other protocols.
4	
5	### 4.1 What it does
6	
7	OUR DESIGN. The loop is for adults on blood-pressure medicine who miss the 30-day review: the half who do not return (chapter 1). Once a month the patient takes a week of home readings with an upper-arm cuff and sends each one as a photo of the cuff's screen. The software checks the readings, asks whether the medicine was taken, and drafts the next step of the state's published protocol, with its reasons. A registered doctor approves, edits or rejects it in one tap, and the patient gets the change in their own language, in the doctor's name. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.
8	
9	The protocol is Gujarat's published ladder: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then raise it to 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg if chlorthalidone is not available), with a re-check after 30 days on each step. After the last step the sheet says: "Check if the patient has been taking medications regularly and correctly. If yes, refer to a specialist." It covers adults over 30. Its safety rules are in chapter 4.7, and every protocol rule in this chapter comes from that sheet [D1-06-F14].
10	
11	### 4.2 The system map
12	
13	A loop that changes treatment has six stages. Open parts already exist for each (Appendix C); the work is joining them with a safety rule at each handover (OUR VIEW).
14	
15	| Stage | Its job | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| Sense | Get a number from the home | Photo of any cuff's screen, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
18	| Check | Was the reading taken properly | Kit-built motion clip plus a phone checklist |
19	| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed step | One file per protocol, run by one `decide()` function |
20	| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
21	| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram chat plus a web form |
22	| Learn | Improve choices from each response | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |
23	
24	![System map of the step loop](adaptive-care-pictures/14-system-map.png)
25	
26	*The six stages of the loop and the technology chosen for each tonight.*
27	
28	The engine is one pure Python function, `decide()` (OUR DESIGN). It reads a protocol file written in YAML (a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with its reasons. It never computes a dose: it can only pick a regimen written in the file. Each number in the file carries the sheet's own words; a value the source does not give is left blank, and the engine refuses that branch until a clinician fills it. No language model sits in the dose path (chapter 2.3 gives the reason); a model only reads the cuff photo and handles translation and speech.
29	
30	### 4.3 The patient side
31	
32	![Patient chat on the phone](adaptive-care-pictures/10-bp-patient-chat.png)
33	
34	*Mock-up with example data.*
35	
36	The patient uses a Telegram chat, or a web form if the chat fails, on a phone that may be a family member's (chapter 1.3). It prompts a measurement, takes a photo or typed reading, asks about tablets and delivers the change.
37	
38	The home-reading rule (OUR DESIGN, from published guidance): on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle the patient takes two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes of seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-02-F10]. A session counts only if both readings pass the quality checks. The engine needs at least 3 valid days and aims for 7, as the European Society of Hypertension advises; the same society says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the International Society of Hypertension [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use the same home line. So a mean at or above 135 systolic or 85 diastolic is "still high"; one session at or above 180 or 110 is "very high".
39	
40	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings at 140/90. **Applying a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** The team says so aloud on the slide, and the threshold stays a value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.
41	
42	The photo is read twice by a vision model, checked against plausible ranges and shown back for the person to confirm; memory screens are rejected. General vision models are untested on cuff screens (chapter 2.3) [D2-02-F8]. A photo cannot prove who measured or when; the clip's time-stamped record (chapter 4.5) narrows that gap without closing it. Typed entry is always built; Bluetooth only if an Omron HEM-7156T is in hand [D2-02-F1].
43
